articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.08501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A critical requirement for MITICA -- a full-scale prototype of the heating Neutral Beam Injectors hosted at the Consorzio RFX Neutral Beam Test Facility for the ITER experiment -- is the capability to withstand a continuous voltage of 1MV across the vacuum gaps insulating the beam source from the grounded vessel. To validate such feature, a dedicated voltage-holding test campaign was conducted throughout 2024 and 2025 using a full-scale mock-up of the beam source. The tests also involved an accurate characterization of the associated breakdown events: vacuum dielectric failures which result in rapid potential drops and generate strong current discharges. This contribution will present a relative time reconstruction architecture based on cost-effective, embedded RedPitaya (Zynq-7000 FPGA) devices repurposed as timing hubs. These nodes function as configurable trigger multiplexers while simultaneously recording trigger signals as transients to facilitate the offline reconstruction of event sequences. The method allows self-calibration through measuring the static intrinsic delays of the optical fibers and internal logics, generating delay offsets to synchronize acquired waveforms across a sparse, connected-graph topology of both acquisition devices and hubs themselves.

articles.title: Decoding Transient X-ray Absorption Spectra of Acetylacetone With Multireference Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Theory
articles.abstract: arXiv:2608.09747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) offers an element- and site-specific probe of coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its interpretation requires methods that can treat multiconfigurational excited states across nonequilibrium nuclear ensembles. Here, we report time-resolved simulations of the acetylacetone (AcAc) transient X-ray absorption spectra by combining surface-hopping dynamics from complete active space second-order perturbation theory with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC). The simulated 20-200 fs spectra show a good agreement with experimental measurements and reveal that the TR-XAS response is governed by continuously evolving distributions of molecular geometries on the singlet potential energy surfaces (S2 and S1). In particular, absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV is enhanced for transient, nearly symmetric proton-sharing configurations, whereas the 284-286 eV profile reflects geometry-dependent C1s excitations modulated by proton transfer, bond alternation, and ring opening. For the long-time T₁ spectrum (7-10 ps), the principal features near 281.4 and 283.8 eV are assigned to central C 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals. Together, our simulations provide a more complete mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation by directly linking ultrafast carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.

articles.title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions in SSBM and Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method for SSBM that Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
articles.abstract: arXiv:2608.12545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In our previous work, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a physics-based simulator for combinatorial optimization problems (SSBM), which exploits a distinctive spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phenomenon identified in a dissipative system exhibiting robust causality described by an iterative equation. We further conducted numerical simulations in which initial fluctuations of distinct patterns were applied to large-scale benchmark problems, and reported that the SSBM exhibits a unique behavior absent in conventional Ising machines: under specific conditions, pseudo-spin patterns progressively converge during the solution-search process and ultimately coalesce into a single pattern, with the cut value of the converged solution reaching 99.7% of the best-known cut value. In the present paper, we elucidate the conditions under which the SSBM can be configured to emulate the behavior of a continuous-variable Ising machine. We further demonstrate that by additionally incorporating an effect analogous to physical annealing into these conditions, the SSBM becomes capable of identifying the best-known cut value for the K₂₀₀₀ benchmark instance.

articles.title: Low-rank approximation of Moment Tensor Potential enables reducing training set size without loss of accuracy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.07372v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this study, we implement a low-rank approximation of Moment Tensor Potential (MTP) based on the tensor train (TT) decomposition. The implemented tensor-factorized MTP (TFMTP) and the original MTP model are actively trained via a MaxVol-based algorithm during molecular dynamics simulations of a four-component molten salt mixture, LiF-NaF-KF (FLiNaK), and geometry optimizations of a five-component equiatomic Mo-Nb-Ta-W-V random alloy. We demonstrate that under a 1.5-fold compression, TFMTP requires two times fewer configurations for fitting than the original MTP model, while maintaining an indistinguishable level of accuracy. These actively trained MTP and TFMTP models are further used to evaluate the density and viscosity of FLiNaK at temperatures ranging from 600 to 1200 K, as well as the elastic constants and bulk modulus of the Mo-Nb-Ta-W-V alloy at zero temperature. For both atomic systems, the differences in physical properties predicted by MTP and TFMTP are negligible.

articles.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks
articles.abstract: arXiv:2506.10135v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Networks can have various types of mesoscale structures. One such structure is core--periphery structure, which consists of sets of densely-connected core nodes and sets of sparsely-connected peripheral nodes. Core nodes are connected densely to other core nodes and are potentially connected densely to peripheral nodes, which are connected sparsely to other nodes. There has been much research on core--periphery structure in time-independent networks, but few core--periphery detection methods have been developed for time-dependent (i.e., ``temporal") networks. Using a multilayer-network representation of temporal networks and an inference approach that employs stochastic block models, we generalize a recent method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure citePolanco23 from time-independent networks to temporal networks. In contrast to ``onion-like'' nested core--periphery structures (where each node is assigned to a group according to how deeply it is nested in a network's core), hierarchical core--periphery structures encompass networks with nested structures, tree-like structures (where any two groups must either be disjoint or have one group as a strict subset of the other group), and general non-nested mesoscale structures (where the group assignments of nodes do not have to be nested in any way). To perform statistical inference and thereby identify hierarchical core--periphery structure, we use a Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. We illustrate our method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure in one synthetic temporal network and two real-world temporal networks, and we discuss the structures that we identify in these networks.

articles.title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.20184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.

articles.title: Cooperative control of dissipative qubits: steering along the fastest dissipative contraction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.30073v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the control of dissipative quantum systems, the slow relaxation modes usually set the ultimate manipulation timescale. We show that this bottleneck can be bypassed when dissipation itself is used as the engine of the transfer. For a qubit with non-unital, anisotropic Bloch relaxation characterized by the ratio κ=T₁/T₂>1, coherent control can only rotate the Bloch vector, whereas the bath alone can change its length. The fastest transfer between two thermal states therefore consists in steering the Bloch vector, at every instant, along the direction in which the bath contracts it most rapidly. This direction is obtained in closed form and lies slightly beyond the equatorial plane. With strong pulses, the resulting minimum transfer time is a fraction of T₂, instead of several T₁ for passive relaxation. With bounded fields, the Pontryagin maximum principle yields a bang--singular--bang synthesis whose singular arc is precisely this fastest-contraction direction, and the minimum time exceeds its strong-pulse limit by a correction inversely proportional to the field amplitude. We also determine the full time--energy Pareto front: moderate accelerations require little energy, and the time optimum lies at its steep, high-energy end. Off-axis targets are treated within the same framework; their only additional benefit is a shorter final rotation. These results apply directly to magnetic-resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers and superconducting qubits, all of which operate deep in the strong-pulse regime.

articles.title: Quadratic Sample Complexity for Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning with Unknown Marginals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the quantifier exists A,forall D, where the realizable distribution and its marginal are unknown, we determine the finite-class sample-complexity exponent for strict replicability: two independent samples and one shared seed must produce identical functions. For ε=δ=ρ=10⁻⁴, the worst case over |H|le M is Θ((log M)²), without iterated logarithms. For dge1, 0<εle1/16, and 0<δ,ρle10⁻³, every randomized, possibly improper learner valid throughout an explicit anchored realizable family requires Ω(d²/(ερ²)) samples. For the full Boolean class P_d, dge2, in the same parameter range, we prove the matching characterization Θ(d²/(ερ²)+ε⁻¹log(1/δ)) using a proper Poissonized ball-sampling algorithm. We also give an explicit proper Gibbs upper bound for every finite measurable Boolean class. Our lower bound uses square-root probabilities and volumetric packing; the Gibbs proof builds on established coupling and generalization identities. Finally, we characterize the known-marginal worst case for P_d, showing why that interface must be kept distinct.

articles.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

articles.title: Active Pilot Sampling for Multi-fidelity Estimation in Stochastic Optimization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic optimization with high-fidelity nonlinear models is often computationally prohibitive because each objective evaluation requires sampling-based uncertainty quantification inside an outer optimization loop. Multi-fidelity estimators, such as approximate control variates (ACV), can reduce this cost by exploiting cheaper low-fidelity models, but they require model-output covariance information to determine control-variate weights and sample allocations. These covariances are generally unknown and must be estimated through pilot sampling. Existing pilot-sampling strategies primarily address one-off estimation and do not exploit the structure of iterative stochastic optimization, where covariance information may vary smoothly across the design domain and can be shared across optimization queries. We propose an active pilot-sampling framework that learns a probabilistic emulator of the model-output covariance matrix using a positive-definite parameterization based on matrix-logarithm-transformed correlations and log standard deviations. The emulator provides design-specific covariance estimates for constructing ACV estimators at new optimization queries, avoiding repeated independent covariance estimation at every design. Active-learning acquisition functions allocate pilot samples to designs where covariance information is most uncertain and most relevant to the outer optimization objective. We demonstrate the method on a four-branch benchmark and a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimal experimental design application for sensor placement and measurement-time selection in a convection-diffusion system. The results show improved optimization performance relative to single-fidelity Monte Carlo and simpler pilot-sampling strategies.

articles.title: From POMDP Theory to Deep RL with Particle Filters
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning in partially observable environments requires inferring hidden states, learning latent dynamics, and planning under the resulting belief. Practical algorithms often solve one aspect of the above pipeline while relying on approximations for the others that are often poorly understood, while existing POMDP theory typically analyzes computationally inefficient theoretical algorithms far from modern deep RL practice. To fill this gap, we propose a practical end-to-end algorithm that approximately solves the hidden state filtering problem via sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), updates a latent dynamics model online, and performs approximate online planning for d steps before bootstrapping leaves with a state-value critic (a QMDP approximation). We analyze each approximation and prove an end-to-end regret bound decomposing the error into model estimation error, particle filter error, Monte Carlo rollout error, and a structural bias term induced by the QMDP approximation controllable by the planning depth that we further analyze in various special cases. The resulting guarantee makes explicit how statistical sample size, particle budget, rollout budget, and planning depth affect performance. We instantiate our algorithm in an MPC-based deep RL framework, demonstrating its practicality on a variety of environments. On a POMDP that satisfies our assumptions, each term of the bound decays at its predicted rate. Our results provide a practical and theoretically grounded route for bridging theory and practice within online decision-making in POMDPs.

articles.title: Stabilizing Filters for Graph Signal Generation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating graph signals is an important task in machine learning, and incorporating the underlying graph into a generative model enables structurally-informed distribution modeling. However, said graph is often noisy or imperfectly estimated, and structural errors can affect the generative process and the resulting signal distribution. While recent work has established stability guarantees for graph neural ordinary differential equations, the robustness of graph-aware reference dynamics, as used in topological Schrödinger bridge models, remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the structural stability of continuous-time generative models whose dynamics combine a graph filter with a learned graph neural network. We first derive a Wasserstein stability bound that quantifies the effect of graph perturbations on the generated signal distributions. Informed by this analysis, we then propose a principled framework for designing graph filters that balance structural stability with induced signal smoothing. We characterize the optimal filter design and provide an explicit family of polynomial filters with provable stability guarantees. Experiments on synthetic graphs and real-world fMRI signals support our theoretical findings, illustrating the enhanced structural stability of the proposed filters while preserving generative performance.

articles.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

articles.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80% of the experts, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

articles.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.

articles.title: INCARBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Configuration in VASP INCAR by Large Language Models
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.23571v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into first-principles computational workflows, yet their ability to configure scientific calculations remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce INCARBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on input configuration for the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) through both configuration generation and repair tasks. Evaluating 19 model configurations reveals substantial capability differences among current frontier models. While several models achieve high semantic and policy accuracy, task-critical correctness remains substantially lower, demonstrating that parameter-level correctness does not necessarily imply scientifically valid configurations. Failure analysis shows that errors concentrate in physically coupled settings involving DFT+U, magnetism, and correlated materials, where multiple constraints must be satisfied simultaneously. Repair evaluation further reveals that correcting incorrect settings and preserving already-valid configurations are distinct capabilities, with configuration preservation remaining a major challenge. These findings establish scientific configuration as a measurable capability of large language models and provide a foundation for developing more reliable AI systems for computational materials science.

articles.title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27026v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.

articles.title: VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models for Offline Goal Reaching
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning enables skill acquisition by reaching any goal from any state without dense rewards. Model-based methods allow for planning by scaling test-time compute to solve complex tasks. Combining both holds appealing promise for pre-training on suboptimal demonstrations and zero-shot adaptation via goal specification and planning. Yet existing methods assume effective planning requires accurate next-state prediction in pixel or latent space. In this work, we show that value prediction is more useful for planning, whereas accurate state prediction is often unnecessary. Our key insight is that offline goal reaching naturally admits a closed-form Monte Carlo return, enabling value regression to replace temporal-difference bootstrapping. We use this return as the sole supervision for latent world models: imagined latents are trained to predict goal-reaching value rather than match future states, implicitly preventing representation collapse. These planning-oriented representations let imperfect world models imagine on the level sets of value field beyond dataset transitions. We then present VPFlow, a value-predictive planner that pairs the world models with a one-step flow policy and plans in its noise space via evolutionary search. It enables policy improvement with imagined generalized advantage and reduces out-of-distribution queries common in action-space planning. On 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, VPFlow surpasses model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points in success rate, respectively, and outperforms latent planners LeWorldModel, PLDM, and TD-MPC2. It achieves this despite a latent prediction error orders of magnitude larger than with state prediction, while minimizing this error lowers success rate. This demonstrates that value-predictive representations, not exact state prediction, are what offline planning requires.

articles.title: Integrity Assessment of Buried Pipelines under Surcharge Loading Based on a GA-BP Neural Network
articles.abstract: To enable rapid integrity assessment of buried natural gas pipelines subjected to construction surcharge loading, a three-dimensional ABAQUS finite element model incorporating nonlinear pipe–soil contact was developed. The model was validated through mesh-independence analysis and comparison with experimental data reported in the literature, yielding a mean error of 6.32%. The results showed pronounced stress variations in the pipeline within the surcharge-loaded region, with the maximum von Mises stress occurring at the pipe bottom. Based on 100 simulation samples generated using Latin hypercube sampling, a GA-BP neural network model was developed to predict the maximum pipeline stress, achieving a R² of 0.9691. An integrity assessment framework was subsequently established by integrating the prediction model with pipeline failure criteria, and stress contour maps were generated to characterize the coupled effects of multiple influencing factors. Engineering application to three in-service pipelines in the Penglai Dengying Block showed that Pipeline No. 3 reached a peak stress of 219.11 MPa, exceeding the allowable stress of 216 MPa and indicating a potential risk of failure. Therefore, surcharge loading should be restricted and appropriate reinforcement measures should be implemented.

articles.title: Bioprocessing of coconut husk to produce second-generation bioethanol using Zymomonas mobilis ZM4
articles.abstract: Coconut husk is an abundant lignocellulosic residue generated by the tropical coconut processing industry and remains largely underutilized despite its high carbohydrate content. However, its recalcitrant structure limits efficient conversion into fermentable sugars and bioethanol. In this study, an integrated strategy involving sequential pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and microbial fermentation was developed for efficient valorization of coconut husk into second-generation bioethanol. Sequential pretreatment using dilute acid, alkaline treatment, and bleaching significantly improved cellulose accessibility, as confirmed by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy analysis. Enzymatic hydrolysis using a cellulase–hemicellulase cocktail released substantial fermentable sugars, yielding approximately 230 mg glucose and 161.25 mg xylose per gram of raw coconut husk. High-performance liquid chromatography analysis confirmed efficient saccharification, corresponding to sugar recovery efficiencies of approximately 50–60% following pretreatment and hydrolysis. Mass balance analysis indicated that enzymatic hydrolysis released 0.23 g glucose g⁻¹ biomass, of which Zymomonas mobilis converted approximately 83% into ethanol, resulting in a final yield of 0.0975 g ethanol g⁻¹ biomass. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of converting coconut husk into fermentable sugars and bioethanol and highlight its potential as a sustainable feedstock for second-generation biofuel production. The integrated bioconversion framework presented here provides insights for improving biomass utilization and supports the development of circular bioeconomy strategies for agricultural residue valorization.

articles.title: Assessment and Evolution of Surface-Subsurface Landform Connectivity of Jabal Al Qarah in Saudi Arabia: A Potential World-Class Geomorphological Heritage
articles.abstract: Worldwide, surface and subsurface connectivity of geomorphic processes, landform diversity, and their geoheritage importance are very interesting topics. Jabal Al Qarah is a mesa (residual hill), located in Al Ahsa, Saudi Arabia. This mesa offers unique diversity in surface and subsurface landforms. Therefore, the scope of this paper is a detailed geomorphological heritage assessment of Jabal Al Qarah, which was a gap. The geomorphological heritage assessment is considered based on scientific and additional value. The key landforms in Jabal Al Qarah are vertical slots, a rill network, a rectangular fault system, a rectangular cave system, a rock pillar, and an in-situ boulder, which belong to the IUCN Geoheritage Theme: Erosional, Cave and Karst System. Jabal Al Qarah comprises a deposition of marine sedimentation, which is followed by the orogeny of the tablelands and plateaus in the eastern part of Saudi Arabia. Due to weathering and denudation, this mesa unit detached from the Shedgum Plateau and formed the mesa. Following the rectangular fault system that is exposed at the surface, weathering forms a rectangular cave system. Jabal Al Qarah is a unique example with spectacular surface and subsurface landform diversity, high representation, well accessible, and a global example of the complex geomorphic process associated with cave formation. Therefore, Jabal Al Qarah is a strong candidate for inclusion in the world-class geomorphological heritage.

articles.title: An Effective Polyamine-Based Coagulation–Flocculation Approach for Cyanide and Color Removal from Steelmaking Wastewater
articles.abstract: The present work demonstrates the usability of organic polymers as coagulant/flocculation aids for successful removal of free cyanide and color from steelmaking industrial wastewater. The effluent was characterized using various analytical instruments and contained a high cyanide concentration of about 13.2 ppm and color intensity of 7350 Pt-Co due to the presence of suspended solids, iron-containing species, and other lipophilic colloids. The treatment process involved the sequential addition of 60 ppm copper sulfate catalyst, 300 ppm sodium metabisulfite, and 400 ppm ferrous sulfate to convert toxic cyanide into less toxic cyanate, followed by coagulation and flocculation. Four different polyamine coagulants with varying molecular architectures were evaluated for treatment performance. Among them, the linear polyamine coagulant PA-L exhibited superior performance compared with branched and highly branched analogues, owing to its enhanced bridging capability and improved accessibility of cationic functional groups. Using an optimum dosage of 100 ppm coagulant followed by 4 ppm anionic flocculant aid, the cyanide concentration was reduced from 13.2 ppm to 0.2 ppm and color from 7350 Pt-Co to 90 Pt-Co, corresponding to removal efficiencies of 98.5% and 98.8%, respectively. The treated effluent satisfied the prescribed discharge limits for cyanide and exhibited excellent clarification characteristics. The study further highlights the influence of polymer architecture on coagulation performance and demonstrates that polyamine-based coagulation–flocculation is a simple, scalable, and economically attractive treatment approach for steelmaking wastewater. Based on the optimized treatment conditions, a scale-up study was successfully carried out for the treatment of actual steel plant wastewater.

articles.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Atom-Resolved VOCs Adsorption and Reactivity on Metal Oxides
articles.abstract: The adsorption and reactivity of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) on metal oxides govern catalytic reaction pathways, yet predictive rules remain elusive because molecular functionality, surface chemistry, and adsorption geometry are strongly coupled. Here we report a transferable adsorption dual-tower framework (AdsDT) that independently encodes molecular and crystal features to predict adsorption energies directly from unrelaxed CIF structures. By pretraining on the Open Catalyst 2020 dataset and progressively transferring through intermediate adsorption systems, AdsDT enables rapid construction of metal oxides-VOCs interaction databases and achieves strong agreement with density functional theory calculations (R2 = 0.85). Using 816 TiO2 (anatase, 101)-VOCs adsorption configurations, we combine molecular fingerprints, SHAP analysis, and graph attention mapping to identify fragment-level and atom-resolved adsorption contribution. Saturated alkyl carbon environments increase predicted adsorption energies, whereas unsaturated and electronegative atoms, particularly carbonyl oxygen, favor stronger adsorption. Extension to eight representative metal oxides reveals material-dependent and functional-group correlation. Furthermore, a bond activation score integrating atomic attention, bond dissociation energy, and bond polarization links adsorption configurations to reaction pathways, showing that adsorption sites activate neighboring bonds through electronic redistribution rather than serving simply as cleavage centers. These results provide transferable atom-resolved descriptors for VOCs adsorption and catalytic reactivity across metal oxides.

articles.title: Chemical and Microstructural Characteristics of Soils Treated with Pulverised Charcoal and Gum Arabic
articles.abstract: Chemical and microstructural characterisation provides a basis for understanding interactions between locally available additives and soil. This study examined pulverised charcoal, gum arabic, and two soils from Ibadan treated with nominal charcoal–gum proportions of 2%–2%, 4%–2%, and 2%–4%. Proximate and ultimate analyses, reported oxide compositions, six X-ray diffraction patterns obtained after 14 days, and twelve scanning electron micrographs assigned to 7 and 14 days were evaluated. Charcoal contained 10.60% moisture, 40.40% volatile matter, 30.75% fixed carbon, and 18.25% ash. The revised oxide entries for gum arabic totalled 92.30%, with a loss on ignition of 7.70%. In treated soils, silica and alumina contents ranged from 49.01 to 56.46% and from 22.02 to 32.10%, respectively. The available oxide entries and loss on ignition summed to 99.97–100.00%, although one phosphate entry was unavailable. Changes between curing ages varied across treatments, indicating contrasting compositional patterns. Diffraction annotations identified quartz, feldspar, mica, kaolinite, and illite, while microscopy descriptions indicated heterogeneous granular, plate-like, and aggregated surfaces. This study provides a preliminary description of the reported analytical entries and author-assigned specimens. Interpretation remains subject to confirmation of the analytical reporting bases and specimen traceability, including a potentially repeated microscopy field. The findings inform further investigation of the combined treatment; confirmation of reaction mechanisms and engineering suitability will require complementary controls and performance testing.

articles.title: Magnet-free reconfigurable alterspin photonics at optical frequencies
articles.abstract: Altermagnetism is a compensated magnetic order in which spin polarization alternates between symmetry-related momenta despite zero net magnetization. Recently, an altermagnetic photonic crystal was demonstrated by mapping electron spin onto light spin, while still relying on gyromagnetic materials and magnetic bias. Hence, it is rather elusive to extend the altermagnetism concept to optical frequencies. Here we realize reconfigurable magnet-free alterspin photonics in an all-dielectric photonic crystal across 740–800 nm. The in-plane square lattice fixes the four-period angular form of the alterspin texture, while an extrinsic out-of-plane dielectric perturbation controls its sign and amplitude. A liquid droplet enables writing, erasing, and reversing the alterspin texture. We further establish a criterion to evaluate the alterspin order and quantify the measured texture. Our results provide a route toward visible-to-near-infrared alterspin photonic systems that are magnet-free and externally reconfigurable.

articles.title: Analytical Modeling of 12/10 stator/rotor pole configuration of Switched Reluctance Motors Considering Magnetic Saturation for Blood Pump Applications
articles.abstract: This paper presents a comparative analytical study of torque ripple and radial force characteristics in 3-, 4-, and 6-phase switched reluctance motors (SRMs) with a 12/10 stator/rotor pole configuration, accounting for magnetic saturation effects. While multi-phase SRMs are generally expected to offer improved torque smoothness over conventional 3-phase designs, a systematic comparison of their torque ripple and radial force behavior particularly under saturated conditions has not been thoroughly investigated in the literature. To address this gap, a unified two-dimensional analytical model is developed based on Fourier series, incorporating saturation effects through a modified flux-linkage characteristic. The model predicts electromagnetic torque and radial force as functions of rotor position and phase current for all three phase configurations, and is validated against finite element simulations. The comparative results reveal distinct performance trends across the different phase numbers, highlighting trade-offs between torque ripple suppression, radial force magnitude, and force ripple. A key contribution of this work is linking radial force behavior to bearingless motor technology, where unbalanced radial forces directly affect rotor suspension stability and increase the control effort required for magnetic levitation. This is particularly critical for blood pump applications, where mechanical oscillations and bearing friction impose excessive mechanical stress on blood cells, increasing the risk of hemolysis. By identifying the optimal phase configuration that minimizes both torque ripple and radial force fluctuations, this study provides a foundation for designing quieter, more reliable bearingless drives with reduced mechanical stress and improved hemocompatibility

articles.title: Dispersive Liquid-Liquid Microextraction for Arsenic Speciation in Complex Food Matrices
articles.abstract: Arsenic is a highly toxic metalloid that poses serious health risks through contaminated food and water. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established ultra-low permissible limits for arsenic, demanding analytical methods with exceptional sensitivity and accuracy. Dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction (DLLME) has emerged as an effective sample preparation technique for arsenic determination and speciation, offering high enrichment factors, rapid extraction, minimal solvent consumption, and operational simplicity. This review presents an overview of recent DLLME-based strategies for arsenic monitoring across food, aqueous, and biological matrices, with particular emphasis on food applications and related analytical challenges. Special emphasis is placed on advanced extraction media including deep eutectic solvents (DESs), ionic liquids (ILs), and magnetic ionic liquids (MILs), often integrated with magnetic solid-phase extraction or automated lab-in-syringe systems. Key performance metrics are compared for total arsenic, inorganic As(III)/As(V), and selected organic arsenic species across food, water, and biological matrices. By critically identifying matrix-specific challenges, speciation-related limitations, and gaps in method standardization, this review provides practical perspectives for developing more reliable DLLME-based strategies for arsenic monitoring through improved analytical approaches for food and water safety.

articles.title: Neural correlates of empathy in autism: a coordinate-based meta-analysis
articles.abstract: Purpose. Autistic and non-autistic people often differ in how readily they understand one another’s intentions and emotional states. Although empathy is commonly invoked to explain these differences, which components of empathic processing differ in autism, and their neural underpinnings, remain unclear. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered coordinate-based meta-analysis (activation likelihood estimation; ALE) of task-based fMRI studies of empathy in autism, examining within-group convergence, conjunction and between-group divergence separately for affective and cognitive components. Eleven studies (12 independent samples) met inclusion criteria, comprising 213 autistic and 216 non-autistic participants and 600 foci across 35 experiments; a multi-agent AI second reviewer supported screening and extraction. Results. Both groups shared a core empathy network (precuneus/posterior cingulate cortex, right middle temporal gyrus/posterior superior temporal sulcus, left inferior frontal gyrus, dorsomedial paracingulate), but the rostral dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, a canonical cognitive-empathy hub, converged only in non-autistic participants. The between-group contrast was strongly asymmetric: non-autistic participants exceeded autistic convergence in ten regions, eight of them cognitive-empathy nodes, the largest in rostral dorsomedial prefrontal cortex; autistic participants exceeded non-autistic convergence in one region only, the posterior right temporoparietal junction. Subdomain analyses indicated relatively preserved convergence for affective empathy, with sparser, more diffuse overlap for cognitive empathy. Conclusion. These findings are consistent with a dissociation between relatively preserved affective and altered cognitive empathy in autism, and suggest a redistribution of activation within the mentalizing network rather than a global absence of empathy-related processing. Key words: autism spectrum disorder; empathy; activation likelihood estimation; functional magnetic resonance imaging; dorsomedial prefrontal cortex; temporoparietal junction

articles.title: A Rule-Breaking Class of Planar Central Chiral Molecules in Planar Tetracoordinate Carbon Systems
articles.abstract: Unusual bonding, stability, and potential applications of planar tetracoordinate carbon (ptC) have captivated researchers over the past five decades. Chirality has been reported in both a central carbon in a non-planar structure and in a planar geometry without a central carbon. Here, for the first time, the present work introduces the concept of planar tetracoordinate chiral carbon (ptCC) systems, in which four distinct ligands create an asymmetric center while maintaining planar tetracoordination at the carbon. This study identifies eight ptC structures that exhibit chirality and form enantiomeric pairs. The chemical bonding and stability of the ptCC structures were analyzed using the Adaptive Natural Density Partitioning, and Electron Localization Function. The aromaticity of ptCC geometries was assessed using nucleus-independent chemical shift analysis. The chirality of the ptCC systems was confirmed by examining their chiroptical properties, as evidenced by electronic circular dichroism and vibrational circular dichroism spectra. The observed chiroptical spectral features show mirror-image profiles for the enantiomeric pairs investigated. As discussed, this rule-breaking class of ptC molecules exhibits chirality at the planar central carbon. The ptCC systems investigated exhibit structural features that suggest potential utility in asymmetric catalysis and materials applications.

articles.title: Inside an Arnoldi Mushroom: Minimally Invasive Multi-Analytical Characterisation of a Nineteenth-Century Papier-Mâché Object
articles.abstract: This work presents the adapted application of X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) for the analysis of painted historical papier-mâché objects, with particular focus on optimising the experimental parameters of the laser-based techniques to minimise potential damage. Mock-ups of the material, featuring different pigment finishes, were used to evaluate the analytical performance of the techniques and assess laser-induced alterations, establishing a balance between analytical signal quality and surface impact. The selected conditions were subsequently applied to a historically significant case study: a 19th-century papier-mâché model of the mushroom Amanita muscaria from the Arnoldi collection. The papier-mâché matrix was attributed to a mixture of a calcium-based component, including gypsum and calcium carbonate, and a silicate-based component, including quartz and kaolin. Red lead, chrome yellow, and a lithopone-based finishing layer were identified as the main pigments and surface treatments. To complement the spectroscopic analysis, ultraviolet-induced visible fluorescence (UVF) photography was used to further characterise specific pigments, while X-ray computed tomography (CT) was employed to non-destructively investigate the internal structure of the object, revealing wooden cores within the mushroom bodies and the depth of fractures. These results provide insights into the materials and conservation state of the model and demonstrate the value of combining complementary analytical techniques for the study and characterisation of fragile cultural heritage objects.Keywords: Papier-mâché, LIBS, Raman spectroscopy, XRF, X-ray CT Scan, Cultural heritage

articles.title: SimuScan-Agent: language-model orchestration of synthetic-data-driven autonomous atomic force microscopy
articles.abstract: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) enables nanoscale characterization, but large-area investigations remain slow and require coordination of data preparation, model training and instrument operation. Here we introduce SimuScan-Agent, an LLM-orchestrated framework that translates natural-language objectives into adaptive AFM workflows. Combining multimodal morphological sources with physics-informed simulation, it generates annotated synthetic datasets without manual per-image labeling, trains and deploys segmentation and representation-learning models, and guides acquisition using online detections and class-specific sampling objectives. In simulations, probabilistic active exploration reduced measurements and sampled area by approximately 71% relative to raster scanning. Experimentally, SimuScan-Agent explored a ~10 mm² region by sampling 17.2% of available positions, estimating class-specific spatial distributions and assembling a morphological library to identify representative and atypical nanostructures. By linking synthetic-data generation, machine learning and adaptive acquisition through natural-language interaction, the framework lowers barriers to goal-directed nanoscale studies and offers a foundation for more intelligent, autonomous AFM systems that adapt experimental decisions to what they learn during measurement.

articles.title: Collaborative Mass Matrix Adaptation for Multi-Chain Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
articles.abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), together with its adaptive variant, the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), is a standard tool for Bayesian posterior inference. In practice, however, its efficiency is often limited by warmup adaptation. In particular, the mass matrix is typically estimated from the trajectory history of a single chain. When the target posterior exhibits strong dependencies or the warmup budget is limited, this estimate can have high variance, leading to inefficient exploration and frequent treedepth saturation. We propose Collaborative NUTS (C-NUTS), a simple yet effective modification that pools gradient and position information across N parallel chains during warmup to construct a numerically stable, pooled covariance estimate for the mass matrix. This approach is particularly effective in the common N < d regime, where instantaneous cross-chain scatter matrices are rank-deficient and naive updates are unstable. To ensure robustness in multimodal targets, C-NUTS incorporates a lightweight safeguard that monitors between-chain dispersion and temporarily reverts to single-chain adaptation when the chains appear excessively separated. Under standard conditions for adaptive MCMC, we show that C-NUTS preserves the correct stationary distribution. Empirically, C-NUTS improves effective sample size per second by up to threefold over Stan’s dense Euclidean metric adaptation on a range of benchmarks, including correlated Gaussian targets, hierarchical models, and high-dimensional regression problems. The largest gains occur at moderate dimensions, approximately 50 sim 200, where single-chain covariance estimates are particularly unstable. These results suggest that sharing warmup information across chains can substantially improve adaptation efficiency without changing the underlying NUTS transition mechanism.

articles.title: Machine-learned potentials link vacancy-dependent copper transport to post-implantation profiles in silicon
articles.abstract: Copper contamination threatens silicon devices because mobile Cu can form electrically active defects and redistribute during thermal processing. Here we combine DFT-informed implantation simulations, an actively learned deep potential (DP) and large-scale molecular dynamics to connect elementary Cu migration with vacancy-dependent transport and annealed depth profiles. The DP reproduces DFT energies and forces with root-mean-square errors of 3.16–3.71 meV/atom and 35.10–88.30 meV/Å, respectively. Nudged-elastic-band calculations yield an interstitial migration barrier of 0.192 eV, close to the DFT value of 0.185 eV, and capture the energetic preference for Cu occupation of a Si vacancy. Across systems containing eight Cu atoms and 0, 2, 4 or 8 Si vacancies, atom-resolved trajectories reveal competition between mobile interstitial Cu and vacancy-associated Cu. Increasing vacancy number raises the prevalence of locally confined Cu and changes the ensemble-averaged transport behaviour. The vacancy-free system has an apparent activation energy of 0.202 eV, comparable in magnitude to reported experimental values of 0.15–0.18 eV. The combined DFT-MD + DP framework also reproduces the principal features of SIMS profiles before and after annealing. Relative to the MC/BCA + KMC workflow assessed here, it reduces mean-normalized NRMSE by 47–61% across the full profiles, with improvements in both the near-surface region and low-concentration tail. By linking Cu–vacancy interactions to measurable redistribution, this framework offers a route to jointly evaluating implantation-induced defects and annealing conditions when seeking to limit mobile Cu and residual Cu–defect complexes in silicon.

articles.title: Monolithic Vertically Stacked Carbon Nanotube Transistor with Emergent Negative Transconductance for Ternary Logic
articles.abstract: Vertical integration offers an opportunity to engineer transistor responses as well as device placement. Here, we demonstrate negative transconductance (NTC) using two carbon nanotube (CNT) network channels monolithically integrated on opposite sides of a common gate. The vertically stacked NTC transistor connects the channels internally through a via and retains three external terminals. Sequential processing yields a lower channel that is electron-dominant ambipolar under top-gate operation after HfO2 deposition, while the subsequently deposited upper channel remains p-type. Their contrasting gate responses shift the current bottleneck between layers, producing a local current peak. Channel geometry and upper-layer CNT density tune this response, yielding an extracted peak-to-valley current ratio above 104 at a drain-voltage magnitude of 0.1 V. Paired with an n-type CNT pull-down transistor, the device enables a ternary inverter at a 3 V supply, with three output states and two voltage-gain peaks exceeding maximum 6. Comparisons across fabricated variants link the NTC profile to intermediate-state formation and reveal a trade-off between static noise margins. These results establish vertical stacking as a route to single-semiconductor transfer-function engineering for ternary logic.

articles.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Synthesis of MXene-Grafted Coconut Husk Activated Carbon for Enhanced Adsorption of Carbamazepine: Batch Study and Optimization
articles.abstract: The presence of multiple pharmaceuticals in the water bodies as waste causes several hazardous environmental effects for both aquatic and terrestrial animals. The present study investigates the potential of novel MXene nanosheet grafted coconut husk-derived activated carbon (AcC/MXene) on the uptake of a pharmaceutical, i.e., carbamazepine, from the experimental solutions. Mxene nanosheet was synthesized from the MAX phase. Coconut husk was pyrolysed at a higher temperature and in an inert atmosphere to synthesise activated carbon, and Mxene nano-sheet was grafted on the activated carbon using ultrasonication and hydrothermal reaction. The highest adsorption capacity of 427.47 mg.g− 1 of the nanocomposite was calculated from the batch adsorption study. The detailed investigation of the physicochemical characteristics of the nanocomposite displayed micropores, a high surface area, with several functional groups responsible for the high uptake of the adsorbate molecule from the experimental solutions. The adsorption process was optimized using response surface methodology (RSM), in which 99.2515% of carbamazepine removal by the AcC/MXene nanocomposite was estimated in optimized conditions. Furthermore, the kinetic analysis and the isotherm analysis of the adsorption process were performed. The thermodynamic analysis revealed that the adsorption process was spontaneous at a negative ΔG value, and the adsorption process was endothermic, as concluded from the positive ΔH value of 59.47836 kJ. mol− 1. In the 7th cycle of the reusability study, 51.018% of the carbamazepine removed from the experimental solutions demonstrated the economic applications in wastewater treatment.

articles.title: Computational fracture modelling of polymer-bonded explosives and solid propellants: A critical review of local and nonlocal continuum formulations and discrete particle approaches
articles.abstract: Fracture behaviour is a critical determinant of the safety, reliability and service life of polymer-bonded explosives (PBXs) and solid propellants. Both are highly filled polymer composites whose damage evolution is governed by heterogeneous particle-binder architectures, rate- and temperature-dependent binders, interfacial debonding, matrix failure and particle or crystal fracture. A broad range of computational methods has been developed to describe crack initiation, propagation, coalescence and fragmentation, but suitability varies with the dominant mechanism, length scale and intended prediction. This paper reviews five approaches: the extended finite element method (XFEM), cohesive zone modelling (CZM), phase-field fracture modelling (PFM), peridynamics (PD) and the discrete element method (DEM). For each, the theoretical foundation, crack representation, numerical implementation, parameter requirements and applications to PBXs and solid propellants are examined, with emphasis on particle-binder debonding, constituent fracture, interacting crack networks, fragmentation and post-failure contact. The comparison indicates that XFEM enables the non-mesh-conforming representation of one or a few discrete sharp cracks; CZM represents progressive separation along predefined or explicitly resolved interfaces; PFM captures distributed nucleation and complex crack topology; PD accommodates dynamic fracture and fragmentation through a nonlocal continuum formulation; and DEM resolves contact-network evolution and particle rearrangement. These capabilities are conditional on compatible constitutive laws, identifiable and appropriately calibrated parameters, verified numerical implementation and solution, and validation against independent local as well as global experimental observables. Prospective hybrid formulations and machine-learning-assisted strategies are also discussed, together with the requirements for conservative coupling, uncertainty quantification and thermo-mechanical-chemical validation. The review provides a comparative basis for selecting and developing fracture models for the safety and structural-integrity assessment of PBXs and solid propellants.

articles.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
articles.abstract: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping.

articles.title: Physicists trap and tame single particle of antimatter for months
articles.abstract: For the first time, Northwestern University physicists have coaxed a single positron—the antimatter counterpart of an electron—into an exquisitely controlled quantum state.

articles.title: Steering electrons with extreme ultraviolet light—team achieves quantum coherent control
articles.abstract: Light is one of the most powerful tools scientists have for probing matter. By interacting with electrons, light reveals how atoms, molecules and materials are structured and how they evolve in time. Highly energetic ultraviolet and X-ray photons are particularly attractive because they can access electrons located close to atomic nuclei, where each chemical element carries its own distinctive electronic fingerprint.

articles.title: Zeeman Quantum Geometry of the Layer Pseudo-spin
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-dimensional layers coupled by position-dependent interlayer tunnelling host a layer pseudo-spin whose polarization is a controllable internal degree of freedom. We introduce the quantum geometry of this layer pseudo-spin: a mixed tensor formed from the interband Berry connection and the layer matrix element, which governs the response to an oscillating in-plane electric field. Because the layer pseudo-spin is an Ising-type scalar invariant under threefold rotation, its selection rules differ from those of a pseudovector spin. In a minimal two-band model, the layer-pseudo-spin quantum metric and Zeeman--Berry curvature are nonzero, while their zone integrals vanish. An in-plane drive therefore leaves the spatially averaged polarization unchanged at linear order but imprints a moiré-periodic intracell pattern, directly imageable by layer-resolved tunnelling. For twisted MoTe₂ bilayer, we quantify the local dipole modulation and identify the rectified, helicity-odd, and third-harmonic channels through which a net response appears at higher order.

articles.title: Achieving ultrahigh-temperature superfluidity in atomic Fermi gases by suppressing pairing fluctuations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-sought goal of both the physics community and the industry. The superfluid transition temperature T_c of a Fermi system initially increases with increasing pairing strength between fermions following the mean-field prediction of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, and is then suppressed by pairing fluctuations as the strength increases further, which prevents T_c from becoming high. Here we propose a mechanism for suppressing pairing fluctuations using the synergy between population imbalance and momentum space confinement in lattice systems, enabling an ultrahigh T_c at moderately strong attraction. We show that in a three-dimensional optical lattice, strong Pauli exclusion between paired and excess majority fermions pushes up the pair excitation energy and suppresses finite-momentum pairing fluctuations. The mechanism is general to any lattice with a finite Brillouin zone; the optimal imbalance is modest (plesssim 0.1), keeping the Zeeman field small and avoiding orbital complications. The gapped pair dispersion at moderate imbalance exponentially suppresses thermal condensate depletion, providing a testable signature. The gapped dispersion, enhanced condensate fraction, and pseudogap reduction are all accessible in present-day experiments. This work opens new avenues toward room-temperature superconductivity.

articles.title: Field Theory of the Gutzwiller Projection
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Gutzwiller projection produces a well-known ansatz for spin-liquid and quantum Hall ground-state wavefunctions that is amenable to numerical simulation, with the Laughlin wavefunction being the most celebrated example. A long-standing issue is the precise relation between the Gutzwiller projection and the closely related parton gauge theory. Here, we clarify this issue by providing a field-theoretic description of the Gutzwiller projection. In a path integral description, the universal physics of the projected state is described in terms of a gauge field supported on a temporal slab of vanishing width ϵ → 0 coupled to the bulk matter fields. We analytically derive the universal physics of various Gutzwiller projected states. Our construction is also applicable to discrete symmetries, and we use it to analyze various projected SPT states. Among our results, we show that the Gutzwiller projection is not a good ansatz for the long-distance properties of U(1) Dirac spin liquids, spinon Fermi surface spin liquids or composite Fermi liquids, and that the Gutzwiller projection of a quantum spin Hall state has only quasi-long range order. In contrast, in examples where the gauge field is gapped, including Laughlin states, Z₂ spin liquids and Luttinger liquids, we show that the slab gauge theory from Gutzwiller projection reproduces the correct universal physics of the full parton gauge theory. We also present a generalization of our field theory that describes G-intertwining defects, with application to self-duality defects of recent theoretical interest.

articles.title: Spectral signatures of hidden order and hidden quantum critical points
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hidden-order phases elude the conventional Ginzburg-Landau framework: although they spontaneously break symmetry, their order remains invisible to standard local two-point correlators. Instead, they are typically characterized by nonlocal (string) order parameters and are believed to underlie a range of exotic quantum states, such as symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases. While hidden correlations have previously been detected through nonlocal observables in quantum gas microscope experiments, in realistic solid-state systems multipoint observables are typically inaccessible and the signatures of hidden order remain largely unexplored. In this work, we show that hidden order in doped spin chains can be directly probed through dynamical two-point response functions measurable by resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and neutron scattering. Focusing on a minimal model, we numerically identify clear spectral fingerprints of both the hidden-order phase, its associated hidden quantum critical point as well as a specific group of gapless SPT phases. Complementing our numerical results with analytical insights, we uncover the microscopic origin of these spectral signatures and demonstrate how they emerge from the interplay between spin and charge degrees of freedom. Together, our results establish spectroscopy as a practical probe of hidden order and gapless SPT phases and provide a unified understanding of the low-energy physics governing these unconventional quantum phases.

articles.title: Stacking-Induced Tuning of a Flat-Band Surface State in NbIrTe4
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ternary layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) offer high tunability and access to correlated and topological states. However, like the broader family of layered TMDCs, their properties are sensitive to stacking order and interlayer coupling. Here, we investigate the electronic structure and surface states of NbIrTe₄, a candidate Weyl semimetal in bulk, and predicted to be a quantum spin Hall insulator in monolayer form. Using scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), and density-functional theory (DFT), we attribute the strong resonance in tunnelling spectroscopy located approximately 8 meV below the Fermi level to a surface-derived flat band which shows sensitivity to the local stacking order at the surface. In regions where the top layer is laterally shifted, tunnelling spectroscopy instead shows a gap-like feature with intensity near the Fermi level shifted in energy. Combining DFT and quasiparticle interference (QPI) measurements, we find this dramatic change in the spectroscopy in the vicinity of the quasi-1D flat-band surface state becomes dispersive due to a change in the spatial distribution of the density of states in the top two layers. These findings establish NbIrTe₄ as a platform where surface band dispersion can be effectively tuned through local structural manipulation.

articles.title: Diffusive Description of Superconducting Single-Photon Detectors Using Quantum Mechanics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The methodology of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics is employed to parameterize the dynamics of coupled classical diffusion equations describing low- and high-energy quasiparticles in superconducting single-photon detectors in one to three spatial dimensions.

articles.title: Nanoscale chemical engineering of Ti3C2Tx MXene multilayers through in situ electron beam irradiation in a TEM
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defect engineering in low-dimensional materials is a powerful approach to tailor their structure and chemistry at the atomic scale, with high relevance for tuning physical properties. Here, we apply this strategy to MXenes, one of the largest families of two-dimensional (2D) materials, and demonstrate the use of a highly focused scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) beam for the structural and chemical nanoengineering of titanium carbide (Ti3C2Tx) multilayers. By adjusting the beam energy, electron dose, and scanning parameters, Ti3C2Tx multilayers were irradiated at 80 and 300 keV and characterized in situ using annular dark-field imaging and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS). The irradiation induces gradual structural and chemical modifications, largely driven by the selective sputtering of atomic species and MXene layers. We identify irradiation conditions that selectively remove Cl or F surface terminations while largely preserving the Ti3C2 framework, whereas other conditions promote preferential carbon removal, in agreement with theoretical predictions. Most notably, electron irradiation drives the migration and accumulation of initially dilute nitrogen impurities within the irradiated regions, leading to the formation of nitrogen-rich titanium carbonitride (Ti3CyNzTx) nanodomains embedded in the Ti3C2Tx multilayers. These laterally patterned carbide/carbonitride architectures constitute in-plane MXene heterostructures with nanometer-scale spatial control. These results demonstrate that electron irradiation can be used to locally tailor MXene composition and create nanoscale architectures beyond those accessible through conventional chemical synthesis.

articles.title: Soft elasticity of soft shells
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.

articles.title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-chip thermal processing is a key technology for materials discovery across all disciplines of the natural sciences. Here, we present a microfabricated heat-delivery platform that enables reaction-induced localized on-chip annealing up to 1400degC. A buried reactive multilayer combined with a nanometric diffusion barrier provide ultra-fast heating and quenching rates on the order of 10⁶degC s⁻¹ as illustrated by the generation of ultra-high aspect ratio microstructures during rapid-solidification and the stabilization of dopant-free tetragonal zirconia at room temperature. Rapid kinetics also enable the observation of transient states of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts. Our work expands localized high-temperature processing routes and offers a material-independent approach for rapid screening of multidimensional nanomaterials on and off-equilibrium.

articles.title: In Situ Thermal Preparation by CO₂-Laser and Chemical Characterization of Oxide Substrates Across Multiple Crystallographic Orientations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomically flat and chemically controlled oxide substrate surfaces are essential for high-quality epitaxial growth of complex materials and heterostructures. Previous studies have demonstrated in situ thermal preparation of selected oxide substrates, primarily focusing on conventional low-index orientations such as SrTiO₃ (100) and LaAlO₃ (100). Here, we extend these methodologies to a broader range of oxide substrates and crystallographic orientations, including challenging polar surfaces. We present a systematic study of the in situ thermal preparation of SrTiO₃ (100), SrTiO₃ (111), GdScO₃ (110), LaAlO₃ (111), (LaAlO₃)₀.₃(Sr₂AlTaO₆)₀.₇ (001), and NdGaO₃ (110) single crystal substrates. The substrates are annealed in a vacuum chamber under a controlled oxygen background environment using a CO₂ laser heating system. The optimized annealing conditions produce atomically flat step-and-terrace structures, long-range surface crystallinity, and effectively clean surfaces across all the investigated substrates. Our results establish a versatile, reproducible, and broadly applicable platform for the in situ preparation of oxide substrates immediately prior to epitaxial growth. These results also provide practical guidelines for interface engineering and surface-sensitive investigations of complex materials.

articles.title: Nanocrystalline cubic boron arsenide growth on GaAs(100) by gas source molecular beam epitaxy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cubic boron arsenide (c-BAs) is a promising ultrahigh thermal conductivity semiconductor, but its direct synthesis on lattice-mismatched substrates remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanocrystalline c-BAs thin films on GaAs(100) substrates using gas source molecular beam epitaxy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals an optimal growth temperature window of 250-400 C to maintain near stoichiometry and suppress severe arsenic loss. Surface and structural characterizations via atomic force microscopy, reflection high-energy electron diffraction, and grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction demonstrate a Volmer-Weber 3D island growth mode and a preferential crystallographic alignment with the GaAs substrate. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy confirms a chemically sharp interface without gallium interdiffusion into the c-BAs layer. These findings establish an initial step for the integration of c-BAs into advanced thermal and optoelectronic platforms.

articles.title: Charge-conserving creation and annihilation of topological phase singularities in atomically thin semiconductors
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides provide a promising material platform for optical phase manipulation, as rapid variations in their dielectric functions can give rise to topological phase singularities (PSs). However, PS evolution while preserving topological charge conservation has not yet been investigated in exciton enabled PS systems. Here, using atomically thin MoS2 films on sapphire as a model system, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate that the evolution of dielectric dispersion determines the creation, trajectory, merging, and annihilation of optical PSs under topological charge conservation. By varying the MoS2 film thickness, we experimentally realize this evolution through the gradual shrinking of the high energy n-k dispersion loop, which modifies its intersection with the zero reflection condition. Our results provide a general strategy for exploring and manipulating topological optical states.

articles.title: Persistent Photo-Enhancement of Molecular Orbital Excitations in the Kondo Insulator FeSb₂
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When insulators are excited by photons with above-gap energies, photo-doped carriers are transiently generated. Typically, orbital excitations weaken and broaden due to increased screening by these transient carriers, followed by a few-ps recovery via phonon thermalization. Here we report the observation of anomalous dynamics of many-body molecular orbital excitations in the narrow-gap Kondo insulator FeSb₂.
