Reliability analysis showed low calibration error under the validation protocol (ECE 0.0095, Brier score 0.0146) and strong error discrimination using detector confidence (AUC 0.9894) and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty (AUC 0.8873). However, zero-shot evaluation on an independent 831-image SIXray-derived subset produced a substantially lower mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.0408 and recall of 0.0954, demonstrating considerable cross-dataset domain shift. Collectively, these findings show that concealment-aware feature enhancement can improve sensitivity and spatial grounding for difficult prohibited-item X-ray cases while providing complementary reliability information. Nevertheless, CAU-XInspect should be regarded as a technical proof of concept rather than an operationally validated security-screening system. Broader cross-scanner validation, domain adaptation, and human-in-the-loop evaluation are required before real-world deployment.

articles.title: American orographic control of simulated Pacific rainfall and warming patterns
articles.abstract: Pacific sea-surface warming patterns influence regional rainfall and the pace of global warming by shaping atmospheric circulation and cloud feedbacks, but climate models still struggle to reproduce Pacific rainfall biases and recent warming patterns. Here we show that one source of these errors is the smoothed representation of the Rockies, Central American cordillera and Andes in coarse-resolution climate models. In experiments that restore more realistic peak elevations, higher American mountains reduce excessive moisture transport from the Atlantic and Amazon regions into the Pacific, weaken the spurious southern tropical rain band and reduce Pacific sea-surface temperature biases. In historical simulations, the same topographic change produces a more realistic recent Pacific warming pattern, especially over the northeastern Pacific, by increasing low-cloud radiative cooling. These results identify smoothed American orography as a physically interpretable and potentially correctable model error with implications for Pacific rainfall, warming-pattern biases, regional climate projections and regional climate risk.

articles.title: A novel biological parcellation of anterior cingulate cortex as identified by a functional reversal point in error monitoring
articles.abstract: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) plays a key role in error monitoring, signalling the need for cognitive control to optimize performance. Although this region comprises multiple subregions, their precise functional organization and contributions to error monitoring remain unclear. We investigated ACC functional parcellation during error monitoring using 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Ten participants performed three variations of a fast-response task: one focused on error commission (without feedback), another on feedback processing, and the last on error observation. We found that distinct ACC subregions were differentially engaged during these processes. Specifically, we identified a polarity reversal in ACC responses to self-generated errors versus correct instances. This reversal separated dorsal subregions ─ more responsive to errors ─ from rostroventral subregions ─ more active during correct outcomes. In contrast, only rostroventral regions differentiated correct from erroneous responses in the observation condition. These findings provide insight into the functional organization of the ACC, suggesting a distinction between dorsal subregions, primarily involved in cognitive aspects of error monitoring, and rostroventral subregions, that may support socioemotional aspects of error processing.

articles.title: Improvement of Biopsy Needle Inner Surface Quality Using Magnetic Abrasive Jet Machining: A CFD-Supported Experimental Study
articles.abstract: In aspiration biopsy procedures, resistance caused by the needle inner surface roughness negatively affects the collection of adequate tissue samples. In this study, in order to solve the problem in question, a unique system was designed and manufactured to polish the inner surface of G14 biopsy needles using the Magnetic Abrasive Jet Machining (MAJM) method. The developed system; It consists of abrasive powder transportation with compressed air, adjustable spindle and neodymium magnet components that move back and forth along the axis. The effects of input speed (50, 75 and 100 m/s) and needle rotation speed (300, 500 and 700 rpm) parameters on surface machining performance were examined within the framework of a 3×3 full factorial experimental design using an abrasive mixture consisting of Al₂O₃, SiC and Fe powders. Numerical analyzes were performed in the ANSYS Fluent environment. The erosion model was carried out using the k-ω SST turbulence model and the Discrete Phase Model (DPM). Erosion rate distributions and particle-wall interaction parameters obtained from CFD simulations were evaluated comparatively with SEM surface images and EDS elemental analyses. Frangi filter-based image processing analysis of SEM images allowed the numerical determination of tangential and radial impact indices. The results show that the inflow velocity is the dominant parameter on the erosion rate; In the transition from 50 m/s to 100 m/s, the SEM region reveals that the average erosion speed increases approximately 5.6 times. When the effect of rotation speed is examined, it is seen that the 500 rpm condition produces the highest tangential scratch density in all speed groups and represents the optimum speed level in terms of homogeneous surface processing. This study presents a novel methodology that combines CFD and SEM image processing, demonstrating the feasibility of the MAJM method in processing the biopsy needles inner surface with numerical and experimental evidence.

articles.title: The Impact of Wintertime NPO on ENSO Triggering
articles.abstract: Recent studies highlight the key role of midlatitude climate variability in modulating tropical El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) activity. This study investigates the impact mechanisms of wintertime North Pacific Oscillation (NPO) in triggering ENSO events in the following year and its dependence on the structural characteristics of the NPO. When the NPO is stronger and located further south, anomalous southwesterly winds in the lower troposphere weaken the background trade winds and enhance local sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies. These SST anomalies are further amplified through the wind–evaporation–SST (WES) feedback, leading to the formation of the North Pacific Meridional Mode (NPMM). Through the seasonal footprinting mechanism (SFM), these SST and wind anomalies propagate toward the tropics, facilitating the westerly wind burst and ENSO onset. In contrast, weaker, more northerly and zonally elongated NPO anomalies confine SST anomalies to the subtropics, where they gradually dissipate. In the upper troposphere, a northeast–southwest tilted NPO-related geopotential height anomaly favors the southward propagation of Rossby wave, supporting the development of tropical anticyclonic circulation anomaly and associated vertical easterly wind shear, which also contribute to ENSO triggering. Therefore, the structure of NPO is crucial for its impact on ENSO. Further analysis reveals that the oceanic feedback can modulate the evolution of NPO structure. The NPO-related wind anomalies adjust air–sea heat exchange and SST patterns, which exert feedback onto the atmosphere by changing diabatic heating and transient eddy forcing. Diabatic heating dominantly contributes to maintaining the circulation anomaly of the NPO at lower layers, while transient eddy vorticity forcing sustains the equivalent barotropic structure of the NPO. These findings clarify the coupled ocean–atmosphere processes linking wintertime NPO to ENSO, providing insights into extratropical–tropical interactions and ENSO predictability.

articles.title: Disorder-Assisted Reduced-State Quantum Metrology in an Inhomogeneous Kerr-Parametric Cavity under Intrinsic Decoherence
articles.abstract: We study an inhomogeneous two-atom Kerr-parametric cavity under Milburn intrinsic decoherence, with particular attention to the distinction between calibrated and uncalibrated static disorder. The Hamiltonian is formulated in the pump rotating frame, uses the standard Kerr interaction χ adagger ²a², and allows independent emitter detunings and coupling variations. All main calculations use a converged photon cutoff n_c=9. For each known disorder realization we evaluate the reduced atomic QFI and then average it, whereas for unknown disorder we first average the density matrices and evaluate the QFI of the mixed ensemble state. These quantities behave very differently: moderate disorder can increase the calibrated realization-averaged QFI, while the QFI accessible without knowledge of the realization decreases as disorder grows, in agreement with QFI convexity. Negativity and coherence are also analyzed, and convergence with both photon cutoff and number of disorder realizations is reported. The results identify a physically meaningful calibrated-disorder localization effect without claiming that unknown disorder creates metrological information.

Haifa S. Alqannas Haifa S. Alqannas

articles.title: Rapid and highly sensitive wide-field quantum microwave imaging via pixel-wise digital lock-in detection
articles.abstract: High-resolution, high-sensitivity microwave (MW) magnetic field imaging is indispensable for non-destructive integrated circuit (IC) testing, radio-frequency device characterization, and spintronic research. Yet, the practical utility of these techniques is severely constrained by the pervasive challenge of isolating weak magnetic signatures from intense optical and electronic noise, which fundamentally limits both acquisition speed and detection sensitivity. Here, we overcome this barrier by introducing a wide-field imaging scheme based on an ensemble of diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, synergistically combined with digital lock-in amplification (DLA). By exploiting digital demodulation, the DLA precisely extracts the MW‑field response at a specific modulation frequency from background noise (e.g., laser intensity fluctuations), dramatically improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Consequently, our system attains a magnetic field sensitivity of 126 nT/Hz1/2. Critically, the unprecedented SNR permits a pixel dwell time of under one millisecond, allowing full-field images to be acquired within seconds-more than an order of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art NV-based wide-field techniques. This combination of speed, sensitivity, and micron-scale spatial resolution (1.6 µm) paves the way for quasi-real-time, non-invasive diagnostics of dynamic MW devices and integrated circuits. MAIN TEXT

articles.title: Time-dependent fluid simulation of negative point-to-plane DC corona discharge: Influence of neutral gas temperature
articles.abstract: Negative DC corona discharges are widely used in electrostatic precipitation, ozone generation, and plasma-based surface treatment. In this study, a time-dependent axisymmetric fluid model is developed in COMSOL Multiphysics to investigate the effect of neutral gas temperature on a negative DC point-to-plane corona in dry atmospheric air. The model solves coupled drift-diffusion and Poisson equations under the local field approximation. Results show that increasing gas temperature reduces the densities of electrons, positive ions, and negative ions, while the electric potential and electron temperature remain relatively insensitive. These findings provide useful guidance for the thermal design of atmospheric-pressure corona devices.

articles.title: Engineering of Giardia lamblia NADH Oxidase: A Single Point Mutation Yields an Efficient Dual-Specific Biocatalyst for Cofactor Regeneration
articles.abstract: Water-forming NADH oxidases (NOXs) are valuable biocatalysts for in situ cofactor regeneration; however, most wild-type NOXs exhibit strict specificity for either NADH or NADPH, limiting their general applicability in redox biotransformations. Although complete reversal of cofactor specificity has been engineered in several NOXs, generating a balanced, "dual-specific" catalyst capable of efficiently utilizing both cofactors is highly desirable for industrial applications. Here, we report the rational engineering of the water-forming NOX from Giardia lamblia (GlNOX). Combining structural modeling with evolutionary sequence alignments, we identified three key residues within the cofactor specificity loop predicted to dictate coenzyme discrimination. Site-directed variants (D180A, G181R, and S182H) were expressed, purified, and structurally characterized by circular dichroism and intrinsic fluorescence spectroscopy, confirming that global protein folding was preserved. Steady-state kinetic analysis revealed that S182H exerted minor effects on catalysis, whereas G181R completely inverted selectivity toward NADPH, albeit at the expense of catalytic rate. In contrast, the single D180A substitution significantly enhanced NADPH utilization while maintaining high catalytic efficiency toward NADH. Electrostatic surface potential mapping confirmed an enlarged, less negatively charged active-site pocket in the D180A variant. Overall, this study demonstrates that a single point mutation guided by in silico modeling can yield a versatile, dual-specific biocatalyst ideal for flexible industrial cofactor regeneration.

articles.title: Molecular substitution controls film connectivity and charge transport in pyrene-based organic field-effect transistors
articles.abstract: Molecular substitution changes both the intrinsic energetics and solid-state organization of organic semiconductors, yet these effects need not produce the same transistor-performance trends. Here, four pyrene derivatives (Py-1–Py-4) are compared in a common top-gate/bottom-contact organic field-effect transistor architecture to identify how molecular energetics, film connectivity, and device resistance jointly influence hole transport. Density functional theory reveals that Py-3 has the lowest adiabatic ionization potential (6.447 eV), whereas Py-2 has the lowest internal hole reorganization energy (0.178 eV), demonstrating that the molecular relaxation-energy ranking does not predict the mobility ranking. X-ray diffraction and electron/atomic-force microscopy show substituent-dependent structural organization, including interconnected fibrillar domains in Py-3 and heterogeneous aggregation in Py-4. Py-3 achieves the highest field-effect mobility (5.4 × 10⁻¹ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹), an on/off ratio of 8.0 × 10⁴, a subthreshold swing of 1.6 V dec⁻¹, and a threshold-voltage hysteresis of 1.1 V. Channel-length-dependent analysis further identifies the lowest contact and sheet resistances for Py-3, while measurements of three devices per derivative support the reproducibility of the performance hierarchy. The results indicate that effective long-range transport depends on connected film morphology and device interfaces as well as favorable molecular energetics.

articles.title: Geometric Foundations of Quantum Entanglement in the Helical-Chain–Biconical Model
articles.abstract: We propose a geometric framework for quantum entanglement based on a helical-chain phase field and a biconical (2:1) transmission ratio. Postulates A1--A7 define the underlying phase field, the (2:1) transmission ratio, the spinor boundary condition, apex-to-apex docking with Fermi statistics, the half-angle measurement projection, an even-(N) tooth-site decoherence potential, and a classical readout rule. Within this postulate system we obtain: the singlet form under a two-sector truncation (Theorem~1); the half-angle probability (P(+)=cos²(θ/2)), hence (E=-cosΔ) and (|S|ₘₐₓ=2sqrt2) (Theorems~2--3); the classical side (|S|le2), independent of (N), under the classical readout (Theorem~4a); for even (N), an (N)-peak structure, peak spacing (2π/N), (τ_dpropto N⁻³), and instanton action ((8/N)sqrtIV₀) (Theorem~4b); the free (K=1) Luttinger-liquid limit corresponding to a Dirac fermion (Theorem~5); the GHZ Mermin quantity (|M|ₘₐₓ=4) (Theorem~6); and the standard W-state reduction ((2/3)|Φ⁺ranglelangleΦ⁺|+(1/3)|00ranglelangle00|) (Theorem~7). We distinguish postulates, theorems, and standard-result correspondences. Under the combined postulates A3--A5, the (2:1) transmission ratio provides a geometric basis for the spinor boundary and the half-angle projection; logical necessity comes from the combination of postulates, not from A2 alone. The tooth number (N) (even) is a replaceable parameter of the decoherence geometry and should be determined experimentally. The present model is an equivalent ontological interpretation of standard quantum mechanics; the (N)-peak decoherence distribution is a candidate distinguishable signal.

articles.title: Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Geothermal Downhole Temperature Prediction Using Hydrogeochemical Datasets
articles.abstract: Accurate estimation of geothermal downhole temperatures is predominantly useful in areas where direct subsurface temperature measurements are limited. This method supports resource assessment and helps to reduce uncertainty during exploration. In this study, we used hydrogeochemical and physicochemical variables to develop and assess machine learning (ML) models to estimate geothermal downhole temperatures in different regions and geological settings. Ridge regression (RR), support vector regression (SVR), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and CatBoost are the ML approaches used in this paper. We assessed model performance through an independent test dataset and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). The predictive performance of the models was evaluated using parameters such as the coefficient of determination (R²), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE). CatBoost achieved the highest overall predictive performance, with a test R² of approximately 0.91 and an RMSE of 23.31°C, whereas Random Forest produced the lowest MAE of 11.21°C and showed close agreement with the ideal 1:1 relationship. Moreover, XGBoost demonstrated strong predictive capability, whereas RR and SVR presented substantially larger prediction errors and greater compression of the temperature range. In addition, LOOCV and residual diagnostics were used to assess model robustness, prediction bias, and temperature-dependent error patterns. The results clearly revealed that ML, especially tree-based models, is an excellent tool for geothermal development where direct subsurface temperature measurements are limited.

articles.title: Sedimentary Fate, Sources, and Ecotoxicological Risk of Persistent Pesticides in the Kol Ramsar Wetland, Southwest India
articles.abstract: The agrarian Kol wetland, a Ramsar-listed wetland ecosystem on the southwest coast of India, is subjected to intensive agricultural activities and seasonal inundation, potentially facilitating the transport and accumulation of pesticide residues in sediments. This study investigated the occurrence, seasonal distribution, vertical transport, persistence, potential sources, and ecotoxicological significance of pesticide residues in surface and sediment-core profiles of the Kol wetland. Organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), including HCH isomers, DDT and its metabolites, dicofol, and butachlor, together with organophosphate pesticides (OPs), including profenofos, ethion, and chlorpyrifos, were detected in surface sediments during wet and dry seasons. The concentrations of ∑DDT were higher during the dry season (31.74 µg/kg) than during the wet season (18.62 µg/kg), with DDE > DDD > DDT indicating substantial transformation and persistence of historical DDT residues. The α-HCH/γ-HCH ratio remained below 3 in both seasons, suggesting additional local inputs of lindane or lindane-related sources. Vertical profiles revealed the occurrence of β-HCH, butachlor, and chlorpyrifos in deeper sediment layers, indicating downward transport and burial associated with seasonal inundation and sediment mixing. Sediment quality assessment identified moderate ecological risks at several surface-sediment sites, while elevated ∑DDE concentrations exceeded the Interim Sediment Quality Guideline at selected locations, indicating potential pressure on benthic organisms. Correlation and positive matrix factorization further indicated mixed anthropogenic sources, including contemporary agricultural inputs, historical pesticide deposition, and monsoonal transport. Overall, the findings demonstrate that pesticide residues persist across the sediment profile of the Kol wetland and may undergo redistribution between surface and deeper sediment compartments. The study highlights the need for systematic pesticide monitoring and improved agricultural management to protect the ecological integrity of this Ramsar wetland.

articles.title: Brain state sets the spatial scale at which cortical geometry constrains human cortical dynamics
articles.abstract: How anatomy constrains large-scale cortical dynamics is contested. Two lines of evidence about what shapes large-scale cortical activity appear to conflict. One holds that geometric eigenmodes of the cortical surface explain brain function more parsimoniously than connectome-derived modes; another holds that long-range connections shape dynamics over and above geometry. We show that neither is categorically right, and that the disagreement dissolves once spatial scale is resolved: connectivity accounts for the broadest cortical patterns and histological geometry for the finer ones. Using cortico-hippocampal neural field models built on ultrahigh-resolution histological geometry and tested against human intracranial recordings and task fMRI, we identify a second constraint. Anatomical pathways are commonly treated as fixed contributions that operate similarly across brain states. Instead, the same hippocampal–entorhinal relay degrades cortical theta organisation during sleep yet supplies it during spatial navigation. Brain state changes the effective spatial scale at which cortical geometry is read out, so anatomy constrains cortical function only jointly with state.

articles.title: Flux-map-based optimal current reference generation for copper-loss minimization and fault-tolerant control of a six-phase electrically excited synchronous motor
articles.abstract: Electrically excited synchronous motors (EESMs) provide an additional degree of freedom through independent rotor-field current, allowing same torque production by multiple combinations of stator d–q, and rotor field currents. However, magnetic saturation complicates the selection of the optimal currents for minimum-copper-loss operation. This paper proposes a variable-field look-up-table (VF-LUT) current-reference generation strategy for six-phase EESM. The LUT is generated offline over the full torque–speed range by optimizing the stator d-q, and rotor field currents subject to torque, current, and voltage constraints based on an experimentally-obtained three-dimensional nonlinear d-q flux-linkage maps to minimize the combined stator and rotor copper losses. The proposed VF-LUT control is experimentally evaluated under healthy and single open phase fault (1OPF) conditions and compared with the conventional FOC and a similar control approach to VF-LUT with constant field current. Over a wide range of healthy operating points, the VF-LUT reduces the total copper loss by an average of 21.9 W relative to the CF-LUT and 8.57 W relative to FOC, with a maximum reduction of 27 W (37%) relative to FOC. 1OPF results further demonstrate continued operation with stable speed and torque regulation, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed VF-LUT control for copper-loss reduction and fault-tolerant six-phase EESM operation.

articles.title: Assessing Climate-Driven Ground Movement Effects on Buried Pipelines Using Efficient 2D and 3D Finite Element Modelling
articles.abstract: Buried pipelines are critical components of UK infrastructure, but they are increasingly exposed to climate-driven soil movement, often resulting in differential settlement. There is therefore a need for computationally efficient tools to support large-scale risk assessment of buried pipelines under changing ground conditions. This study investigated whether a two-dimensional (2D) modelling approach can reproduce the key soil–pipe interaction behaviour predicted by a calibrated three-dimensional (3D) model under varying soil moisture conditions. A parametric analysis was carried out in PLAXIS 3D, which served as the high-fidelity reference model for the soil–structure interaction. The 3D model was first calibrated against experimental data for a concrete pipe and then used in a parametric study in which the water content within an active zone above and around the pipe was varied between 26% and 32%. In parallel, a two-dimensional (2D) finite element model (FEM) was developed in Python and can produce results within seconds. Comparative analysis indicates that the simplified model reproduces the displacement trends and magnitudes obtained from PLAXIS 3D simulations while reducing the computational cost by two orders of magnitude, highlighting its potential for large-scale climate resilience assessment of buried pipeline networks.

articles.title: Using a modified Cavendish experiment to measure dynamics of unexpected effect thanks to modern technology
articles.abstract: We present the results of our measurements of the dynamics of an unexpected effect, which we have provisionally namedthe electromagnetic-gravity effect. These results are compared with those of the interaction of the Coulomb force. Thesemeasurements were performed using a modified Cavendish experiment controlled by computers. The results of thesemeasurements were then compared with each other, with Newton’s laws, with a numerical simulation and with the gravitationalhypothesis. Reference experiments using high-voltage electrostatic stimulation agree with Newton’s laws and numericalsimulations with acceptable accuracy. However, experiments involving the unexpected effect produced significantly differentresults. These results partially agree with the gravitational hypothesis and the numerical simulations based on it. The timing ofthe periodic stimulation differs significantly, by a quarter of a period; that is to say, the phase differs by 90 degrees from that ofthe reference experiments and the results of the numerical simulations. This difference is reproducible. So far, it has not beenpossible to explain this using known physical laws.

articles.title: Refined Gradient-Based Temperature Optimization for the Replica-Exchange Monte-Carlo Method
articles.abstract: arXiv:2601.13542v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The replica-exchange Monte-Carlo (RXMC) method is a powerful Markov-chain Monte-Carlo algorithm for sampling from multi-modal distributions, which are challenging for conventional methods. The sampling efficiency of the RXMC method depends highly on the selection of the temperatures, and finding optimal temperatures remains a challenge. In this study, we propose a refined online temperature selection method by extending the gradient-based optimization framework proposed previously. Building upon the existing temperature update approach, we introduce a reparameterization technique to strictly enforce physical constraints, such as the monotonic ordering of inverse temperatures, which were not explicitly addressed in the original formulation. The proposed method defines the variance of acceptance rates between adjacent replicas as a loss function, estimates its gradient using differential information from the sampling process, and optimizes the temperatures via gradient descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on benchmark spin systems, including the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising model, the two-dimensional ferromagnetic XY model, and the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model. Our results show that the method successfully achieves uniform acceptance rates and reduces round-trip times across the temperature space. Furthermore, our proposed method offers a significant advantage over recently proposed policy gradient method that require careful hyperparameter tuning, while simultaneously preventing the constraint violations that destabilize optimization.

articles.title: Relaxation Dynamics of Superconducting/Normal Interfaces in the Intermediate State of a type-I superconductor
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.17333v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dynamics of phase boundaries, such as superconducting/normal (S/N) interfaces in type-I superconductors, are typically obscured in conventional magnetic measurements, which are strongly influenced by surface barriers and global flux processes. Here, we employ the complex ac magnetostrictive coefficient as a sensitive probe of the bulk dynamics of S/N interfaces in the intermediate state of lead. The ac magnetostrictive coefficient exhibits an unusual complex response, with a negative real component and a positive imaginary component. Frequency-dependent measurements show that the magnitude of the real component decreases monotonically with increasing frequency, whereas the imaginary component first increases, reaches a broad maximum, and then decreases. In contrast, ac susceptibility displays a conventional Debye-type magnetic relaxation with a different phase relation between its real and imaginary components. We propose that the magnetostrictive response arises from ac-field-driven relaxation and rearrangement of metastable S/N domain configurations toward states of lower free energy. These results reveal a distinct interfacial relaxation channel in the intermediate state and establish the complex ac magnetostrictive coefficient as a sensitive probe of nonequilibrium S/N interface dynamics.

articles.title: Data-Efficient Indentation Size Effect Mitigation in Steels Using Machine Learning and a Physics-Constrained Neural Network
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.27775v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Shallow nanoindentation, needed for thin layers, individual phases and small volumes, gives hardness inflated by the indentation size effect (ISE). The Nix-Gao correction reduces this inflation but requires deep indentations of the same material, often impossible in such samples. We present a data-efficient workflow, trained on a few reference materials, that predicts a high-load reference hardness from a single shallow indentation. Seven models were trained on 703 indentations (5-350 mN) on three steels (2.0-6.5 GPa): Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, two feed-forward networks, and two physics-constrained neural networks (PCNNs) that apply a bounded learned correction q as H_app/sqrt(1+q). Over five seeds, models were tested on an external steel not used for training and indented at different loads, in leave-one-steel-out folds, and on fused silica, an out-of-domain material where all models failed. Random Forest and XGBoost, the best on the development set, transferred worst over all loads (MAPE 10.2 and 8.5%), whereas Ridge regression, the PCNNs and one feed-forward network reached 3.7-4.8%; with three training steels, development-set accuracy thus did not indicate accuracy on an unseen steel. From only the external steel's 3-15 mN indentations, the smooth (non-tree) models estimated the reference within 0.03-0.19 GPa on average. The PCNNs matched the linear baseline within the training hardness range and were the most accurate for a held-out steel softer than the training steels, but failed for a harder one. The workflow uses no steel-specific inputs and can be retrained for other material classes.

articles.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives
articles.abstract: arXiv:2605.05104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Materials science data collection can be expensive, making dataset reuse and long-term utility important for future discovery. In practice, data collection often prioritizes properties of current interest while other properties are excluded from the acquisition process. This can produce datasets that are well suited for current objectives but lose information needed for properties of future interest. Here, we present how to construct datasets that remain informative for both. We develop and evaluate acquisition frameworks that combine predictive disagreement with diversity in material features, predicted outcomes, or both. We test these approaches across four DFT datasets and an experimental thermoelectric dataset. Diversity inclusion in dataset construction can reduce present and future objectives trade-off by preserving a broader range of materials and property behavior during acquisition. Across all datasets, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II with disagreements and feature diversity (NSGA-II Dis. + diversity) framework developed in this work provides the most robust balance between current and future objectives. It maintains prediction performance above random sampling for current objectives while mitigating bias on excluded properties and, in many cases, improving their performance beyond random sampling. This diversity-aware acquisition framework provides a practical route to building materials datasets with unbiased quality entries and mitigating cold-start limitations in subsequent modeling and discovery campaigns.

articles.title: Algebraic Structure of Finite-Size Bethe Solutions in the Heisenberg Chain
articles.abstract: arXiv:2605.05589v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain is the canonical example of an integrable quantum many-body model. Despite its exact solvability, explicit finite-size solutions are typically only accessible via numerical evaluation of the Bethe ansatz equations. Here, we analyse the algebraic structure of the exact, symbolic ground states for chains up to twelve sites using the Bethe ansatz. We find that the algebraic degree of the ground state magnon phases and Bethe roots scale with respect to system size at a different rate to the ground-state energy and wavefunction coefficients. The ground-state Bethe roots and energy are found to become Galois unsolvable for ten or more sites, thus demonstrating the lack of a symbolic analytical solution in a quantum integrable model due to algebraic complexity.

articles.title: On the bottom-up construction of many-electron relativistic QED Hamiltonian
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.15040v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It was shown more than a decade ago [J. Chem. Phys. 139, 014108 (2013)] that a many-electron relativistic quantum electrodynamics (QED) Hamiltonian for high-precision electronic structure calculations can be constructed in a bottom-up fashion, by virtue of charge-conjugated contraction (CCC) of fermion operators when normal-ordering the starting unbounded relativistic Hamiltonian (second-quantized in terms of the electronic Dirac field) with respect to the filled negative-energy Dirac sea of electrons. It is shown here that the same relativistic QED Hamiltonian can also be obtained by equal average of the two relativistic Hamiltonians resulting from the normal-ordering of the starting unbounded relativistic Hamiltonians (second-quantized in terms of the electronic and positronic Dirac fields, respectively) with respect to the filled negative-energy Dirac seas of electrons and positrons, respectively, via the standard contraction of fermion operators. In essence, both procedures incorporate properly the fundamental charge-conjugation symmetry of relativistic quantum mechanics to ensure the symmetric treatment of the electronic and positronic degrees of freedom.

articles.title: A fast summation method for the DFT-D3 dispersion correction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.15103v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The DFT-D3 dispersion correction is routinely added to machine learning force fields (MLFFs) trained on dispersion-deficient functionals such as PBE. Its environment-dependent pair coefficients, however, break the atom-centered separability that fast summation methods require, forcing practitioners either to truncate D3 or to accept a substantial slowdown. We introduce FourierD3, a method that uses a functional low-rank decomposition to restore this separability and enable particle-mesh evaluation in O(Nlog N) time without a real-space cutoff on the dispersion sum.

articles.title: Smoothed truncated Coulomb potential for periodic Gaussian-basis Hartree--Fock exchange
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.00203v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Truncated Coulomb (TC) potentials reduce finite-size errors and accelerate thermodynamic-limit convergence in periodic Hartree--Fock (HF) calculations, but their use with Gaussian basis sets is complicated by the evaluation of electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), particularly for nonspherical truncation domains and all-electron calculations. We introduce the smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential as a systematically improvable approximation to a parent TC potential. A real-space Gaussian convolution smooths the sharp truncation boundary, and a single dimensionless parameter, η, controls the width of the smoothing window, which can be tightened to systematically approach the TC reference. The smoothing by sTC enables a dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis ERIs that requires neither a large plane-wave basis nor new molecular integral kernels and is applicable to both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations, including the important Wigner--Seitz-cell truncation boundaries. Benchmarks spanning insulating, semiconducting, layered, metallic, and molecular-crystal systems show that sTC-based HF closely reproduces TC results in pseudopotential calculations and extends TC-quality calculations to all-electron settings. Across these systems, sTC substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence relative to the probe-charge Ewald method while remaining practical for all-electron calculations in which direct TC-based calculations are computationally challenging.

articles.title: Theoretical study of nitrogen-vacancy spin coherence enhanced by vacancy aggregation in diamond using cluster-correlation expansion
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.24295v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Annealing a semiconductor makes its vacancies mobile; they aggregate into multi-vacancy complexes that often carry spin. Such centres are a magnetic-noise source for any spin qubit among them, in silicon and silicon carbide as well as in diamond, and they are accordingly blamed for NV- decoherence in irradiated and implanted diamond, with two coherence records credited to removing them. Cluster-correlation-expansion simulations driven by published electron-paramagnetic-resonance parameters invert that attribution. At a fixed paramagnetic spin density a multi-vacancy bath gives a Hahn-echo coherence time 3.1-7.1 times longer than a bath of isolated negative vacancies, over three decades of concentration. A bath dephases the qubit because its spins exchange spin projections with one another, and two can exchange only if their transition frequencies match. A fine-structure splitting shifts those frequencies. Were every defect on the same crystallographic site, all would shift alike and still match: worth only a factor 1.15. Real defects occupy symmetry-equivalent sites pointing in different directions, so neighbours land at different frequencies and stop exchanging: a further 2.7. What governs the coherence time is therefore the fraction of bath pairs sharing a transition frequency, not the zero-field splitting. Vacancy aggregation extends NV- spin coherence rather than shortening it.

articles.title: Symmetry-Adapted Eigensolver from Real-Space Sampling of Tensor-Network-Bridged Quantum Circuits
articles.abstract: arXiv:2510.19219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a symmetry-adapted eigensolver for strongly correlated systems that separates where the wave function is emphsampled from where it is emphdefined. The lattice is divided into equal blocks: parallel quantum circuits absorb the entanglement within each block, while a matrix product state (MPS) backbone bridges the blocks and restores global correlations. The resulting real-space amplitude φ(aᵣₘ ᵣₑₐₗ) acts only as a sample generator---configurations are drawn from |φ(aᵣₘ ᵣₑₐₗ)|² directly, block by block, without any Markov chain. The variational state itself is defined in a symmetry-adapted basis by two separate rules: the modulus of ψ(aᵣₘ ₛyₘₘ) is the square root of the total weight accumulated over the entire equivalence class, widetildep(aᵣₘ ₛyₘₘ)=sumₐᵣₘ ᵣₑₐₗᵢₙg ₐᵣₘ ᵣₑₚᵣ|φ(aᵣₘ ᵣₑₐₗ)|², whereas its phase is inherited from the single representative amplitude φ(aᵣₘ ᵣₑₚᵣ). The modulus rule is what makes the scheme both exact and cheap: the distributionwidetildep(aᵣₘ ₛyₘₘ) sampled in the symmetric basis is exactly the one induced by the mapping from the real-space distribution p(aᵣₘ ᵣₑₐₗ), so every generated configuration is an unbiased sample of |ψ(aᵣₘ ₛyₘₘ)|²; the phase rule then fixes the only freedom that remains. Because amplitudes within a class are combined in probability rather than summed with symmetry characters, ψ is emphnot a group projection of the circuit-MPS state; the class-wide aggregation instead supplies long-range, symmetry-enforced entanglement that the MPS never has to carry itself.

articles.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
articles.abstract: arXiv:2602.01176v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy ε by the factor κ²γ, where κ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and γ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least 1-α in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.

articles.title: A Unified Physics-Informed Neural Network for Modeling Coupled Electro- and Elastodynamic Wave Propagation Using Three-Stage Loss Optimization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2602.13811v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks present a novel approach in SciML that integrates physical laws in the form of partial differential equations directly into the NN through soft constraints in the loss function. This work studies the application of PINNs to solve a one dimensional coupled electro-elastodynamic system modeling linear piezoelectricity in stress-charge form, governed by elastodynamic and electrodynamic equations. Our simulation employs a feedforward architecture, mapping space-time coordinates to mechanical displacement and electric potential. Our PINN model achieved global relative L2 errors of 2.34 and 4.87 percent for displacement and electric potential respectively. The results validate PINNs as effective mesh free solvers for coupled time-dependent PDE systems, though challenges remain regarding error accumulation and stiffness in coupled eigenvalue systems.

articles.title: Quantum matter is weakly entangled at low energies
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.14143v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct upper bounds on entanglement entropies of many-body quantum states that have fixed energy expectation values with respect to local Hamiltonians. Our focus is on entanglement entropies of subsystems that make up approximately half of the full system. The upper bound on the von Neumann entanglement entropy is half the sum of the thermal entropies of two fictitious systems at the same temperature as one another, with an additional area-law contribution in some systems. The effective temperature is chosen such that the sum of the thermal energies of the two fictitious systems matches the constraint on the energy of the state in the original problem; at subextensive energies, this temperature decreases with increasing system size. Our upper bounds on Rényi entanglement entropies take an analogous form. These inequalities show that, in systems that are frustration-free (FF) and whose zero-temperature subsystem thermal entropies scale with surface areas (rather than subsystem volumes), ground states are area-law entangled. For physical models of quantum matter, which have well-defined specific heat capacities (and are not necessarily FF), our bounds provide a way to convert this thermodynamic data into constraints on pure-state entanglement at both subextensive and extensive energies. We also show that our general upper bounds on half-system entanglement entropies are optimal, up to subleading corrections, in systems with reflection symmetry and above a subextensive energy threshold. A key application of our results is to constrain the entanglement of quantum states relevant to simulations of zero-temperature response functions, which have energies of order unity. We prove that, in wide varieties of FF systems in two dimensions and higher, the contributions of excitations to von Neumann entanglement entropy are subleading compared with the contribution from the ground state.

articles.title: Emergence of Open Chemical Reaction Network Thermodynamics within Closed Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.14848v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Under which conditions do the dynamics and thermodynamics of open chemical reaction networks (CRNs), grounded on the notion of idealized chemostats that exchange selected species, emerge from underlying closed CRNs? While open CRNs provide the standard framework to describe out-of-equilibrium chemical systems, real systems are finite and ultimately relax to equilibrium, leaving the status of this description conceptually unresolved. Here, we address this fundamental question. We show that open-CRN behavior arises as an asymptotic regime of closed CRNs when two physically minimal and transparent conditions are met: a time-scale separation, whereby fast reactions effectively act as exchange mechanisms, and an abundance separation, whereby a subset of species behaves as chemostats with diverging chemical capacity. In this regime, both the stochastic dynamics and the thermodynamic structure - including local detailed balance, entropy production, and free-energy balance - emerge to leading order from the underlying closed CRN. We further predict that this regime persists up to a characteristic time proportional to the scale of the abundance separation, thereby providing an experimentally accessible criterion for estimating how long a finite closed system behaves as an open CRN. Our results apply to arbitrary stoichiometries. They show that chemostats need not be introduced as external idealizations, but instead arise as emergent thermodynamic structures within closed systems, providing a unified and physically grounded foundation for the nonequilibrium thermodynamics of CRNs.

articles.title: AutoREC: A reinforcement learning platform for equivalent circuit model generation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.27266v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces AutoREC, an open-source Python platform for developing, training and evaluating reinforcement learning (RL) agents that automatically generate equivalent circuit models (ECMs) from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) data. Although ECMs are widely used to interpret EIS measurements, their identification typically relies on manual trial-and-error, requiring domain expertise and limiting scalability, particularly in autonomous experimental pipelines such as self-driving laboratories. In AutoREC, ECM generation is formulated as a Markov decision process in which an RL agent sequentially modifies a circuit topology based on the current state, available actions and feedback from the resulting model. The platform supports an end-to-end workflow encompassing EIS preprocessing with selectable impedance representations, agent setup and training, ECM generation for new measurements and visualization-based evaluation and analysis of agent decision-making. AutoREC implements a configurable Double Deep Q-Network agent with prioritized experience replay and a dedicated deadloop mitigation strategy for navigating the complex circuit-generation action space efficiently. To demonstrate the platform, we trained a representative agent on 1350 synthetic spectra from five reference circuit families, evaluated it on 150 held-out synthetic spectra and applied it to 32 previously unseen experimental spectra from battery, corrosion, oxygen evolution reaction and CO2 reduction systems. These case studies illustrate the end-to-end capabilities of AutoREC while revealing challenges associated with experimental complexity and limited training-data coverage. The demonstrated agent serves as a reference implementation; AutoREC provides an extensible foundation through which users can develop and evaluate agents tailored to their specific electrochemical systems and research objectives.

articles.title: AI estimation of partition functions with the PULSE method for the thermodynamic properties of disordered compounds
articles.abstract: arXiv:2605.28594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting the thermodynamic properties of chemically disordered materials is constrained by the combinatorial growth of possible atomic configurations, which makes conventional sampling approaches computationally costly. In this work, we extend the PULSE (Partition function Unsupervised Learning Sampling and Evaluation) approach that enables the estimation of observable-dependent partition functions, thereby extending its applicability from local atomic quantities to general thermodynamic observables. This is based on a generative machine-learning approach in which a single model both generates statistically representative atomic configurations and provides explicit partition function estimates. Our primary goal is to assess it on the two-dimensional Ising model, an exactly solvable benchmark system sharing the same statistical-mechanical formulation as chemically disordered binary materials, and compare its performance against exact brute-force calculations as well as Wolff and Wang-Landau Monte Carlo algorithms. PULSE reproduces the relevant partition functions accurately using a limited number of configurations, at a sampling cost that does not grow with system size. These key results demonstrate the relevance of our method to enable the study of disordered materials at scales that are difficult to achieve using conventional approaches, and with limited computational effort.

articles.title: Learning Effective Bulk Fields from Fermionic Spectra: Application to an Extended Power-Law Liquid Model for Cuprate Strange Metals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.02861v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a Neural-ODE framework to infer effective bulk metric functions and the charge-weighted gauge potential from boundary fermionic spectra within a static, planar black-hole ansatz. Controlled benchmarks recover the known bulk profiles of the Einstein--Maxwell and Gubser--Rocha models. We then use normalized interaction self-energy targets generated from an extended power-law liquid model with parameters calibrated by angle-resolved photoemission measurements to test the proposed geometric explanation of cuprate strange-metal spectra in a semi-holographic setting. For this application, we use a massless probe in backgrounds with conformal-to-AdS₂timesR² asymptotics and derive a spectral extraction formula from the conserved radial Dirac flux. We identify coordinate/Weyl redundancy and a degeneracy in the scaled Hawking temperature of the normalized inverse problem. The conformal factor remains undetermined, so bulk entropy and the associated contribution to electronic specific heat require independent input. Low-temperature targets are fitted accurately across the studied doping range. In the high-temperature test, however, the present ansatz and optimization search have not yielded a refined geometry that accurately reproduces the thermal spectral shape while preserving frequency symmetry. These results may guide the further development of semi-holographic models for cuprates, and the framework may also find applications in other strongly correlated electron systems.

articles.title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.13688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE² simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 43% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.

articles.title: Lattice Boltzmann Methods for Navier-Stokes Equations in General Orthogonal Coordinates for Efficient Flow Simulations using Nonuniform Clustered Grids
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.15362v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Resolving multiscale fluid flows or boundary layers effectively requires the use of nonuniform meshes with local grid clustering. The standard lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), a kinetic theory-based approach for computational fluid dynamics, however, is restricted to the use of uniform Cartesian grids. We present new and improved formulations of the LBM that accommodate continuously varying spatial grids via coordinate transformations to simulate the Navier-Stokes equations (NSE) in the general orthogonal coordinates (GOC). They are constructed using a Chapman-Enskog analysis to specify the equilibrium moments of the distribution functions and the geometric force terms used in the collision step to be dependent on the local metric factors and their spatial derivatives, along with the density, momentum and their fluxes, and some correction terms related to the normal velocity gradients so as to accurately represent the NSE in the GOC. The resulting GOC-LBM importantly maintains the simplicity of the collide-and-stream approach and is Galilean invariant that is free of the cubic velocity artifacts. Our GOC-LBM is general and modular in that it can be used with any collision model with appropriate modifications to the equilibria and forcing terms. We present its implementation details for a variety of collision models while the central moments-based model using multiple relaxation times was found to be the most robust in practical implementations. We validate the GOC-LBM through numerical simulations for various benchmark flow problems. Moreover, we demonstrate significant computational advantages of our approach for a case study on simulating boundary layer flows efficiently that involves coupling the GOC-LBM for the NSE with a new GOC-LB scheme for solving the magnetic induction equation for magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), and for another case study involving orthogonal curvilinear grids.

articles.title: STORM: RDMA-based Monte Carlo Transport Scheme for Distributed-Memory Particle Simulations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.20639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Monte Carlo particle transport enables high-fidelity astrophysical radiation and neutrino simulations - from core-collapse supernovae and neutron-star mergers to accretion flows - by handling multidimensional geometries, frequency dependence, and moving media without angular discretization. However, inter-rank communication limits scalability on unstructured meshes: standard two-sided MPI requires receivers to post receives and poll completions, creating per-iteration progress overhead that grows with the number of communication partners. Such problems have not demonstrated high scaling efficiency at O(10⁴) cores. We present STORM (Scalable Transport via One-sided Remote Memory), an open-source library for Monte Carlo transport on general meshes, physics, and boundary conditions. STORM provides a lock-free, mesh-independent communication layer that replaces MPI's matched-send/receive semantics with Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) - one-sided operations that write directly into a remote rank's memory without involving its CPU. Each rank pair shares a single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer; RDMA writes transfer particles while receivers remain passive. A two-sided MPI backend provides a portable fallback. In an adversarial uniform-emission benchmark, the RDMA backend sustains >97% weak-scaling and >88% strong-scaling efficiency up to 13,440~cores (112~cores per network adapter), with 1.14-1.27× speedups over the two-sided alternative. In a Hohlraum IMC benchmark at 4480 ranks, it is 1.41× faster because MPI progress overhead is reduced by 6.1×. By decoupling communication from physics models and mesh representations, STORM removes a barrier to scaling Monte Carlo transport in astrophysical multiphysics codes, enabling coupled radiation-hydrodynamics with energy- and angle-resolved photon or neutrino transport on dynamically evolving meshes at scale.

articles.title: Picosecond-resolved entanglement distribution over an urban free-space channel
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.21093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

articles.title: Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2608.25631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator for gradient-based learning through exact simulations of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). These models describe discrete stochastic dynamics across physics, chemistry, and biology, but their categorical event choices prevent ordinary differentiation. PST preserves exact forward trajectories and differentiates, in the backward pass, the normalized reaction propensities the simulator already computes. The affine state update makes this rule exact for the one-step conditional-mean sensitivity. We derive the per-step discrepancy for one-step sensitivities composed along nonlinear trajectories in closed form, show that it vanishes for affine downstream dependence, and bound it quadratically in the stoichiometric jump size. Across reversible dimerization, a genetic oscillator, a 50-task repressilator suite, and experimental patch-clamp recordings, PST recovers parameters to within 0.06-1.7% and converges 2.4-3.0-fold faster than the Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator at matched computational cost. At deep-learning scale, PST trains all 203,796 parameters of a stochastic reaction network using exact discrete events from initialization. By differentiating an exact conditional mean, PST eliminates reaction-selection temperature tuning and provides a scalable route to learning through exact stochastic dynamics.

articles.title: Broadband and Large-Multimode Quantum Optical Storage with Rare-Earth Ions in Solids
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.28271v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Broadband quantum memory devices are essential elements for future quantum networks. Here we propose a broadband quantum memory scheme called Hole Anti-hole Grating Echo Memory (HAGEM) for rare-earth ions in solids, which can be implemented with most of the present rare-earth ions hosted in various types of solids. Using HAGEM, a quantum memory device with one billion temporal modes per second can be developed with current available technologies. To validate the memory protocol, we conducted some proof-of-concept experiments. We provide a Eu^text3+ molecular complex with special hyperfine level structures of which the hyperfine level separations are in a specific mathematical correlation that can be obtained by harnessing chemical engineering. Using the proposed memory protocol and material, we experimentally demonstrate a single-mode quantum optical storage efficiency of 14.9% and a memory bandwidth of 200MHz, which can easily be extended to a few GHz. In addition, a multi-mode storage of four temporal modes is achieved with a storage efficiency of 1.3%. Broadband & large-multimode quantum memory device with a long storage time enabled by HAGEM integrating with the current available entangled photon pair source and tunable delay lines, a quantum repeater network with an entanglement distribution rate on the order of 1kHz - 10kHz can be created with a communication distance around 100km. This will greatly facilitate the development of quantum networks in near future.

articles.title: Quantum probability can't be derived without assuming it first
articles.abstract: For nearly a century, physicists have relied on the Born rule to calculate the chances of different outcomes when they measure a quantum system. Yet despite decades of effort, nobody has managed to derive the rule from more basic mathematical principles without making assumptions about probability along the way.

articles.title: A quantum pathway to entropy-free energy transfer
articles.abstract: For scientists, breakthroughs often stem from unexpected turns. A research team led by Oscar Dahlsten, an associate professor in the Department of Physics at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), set out to prove a theoretical limitation, only to discover a quantum solution. The finding breaks traditional physical constraints and introduces a strategy for harvesting energy from fluctuating sources.

articles.title: Scientists redetermine a key strontium frequency with 50 times better precision for quantum technologies
articles.abstract: The Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) has remeasured a key transition frequency of the strontium (Sr) atom for the first time in 88 years, since 1938, using a photonic grating chip. It has established a new absolute frequency value with a measurement uncertainty reduced by more than 50 times. By providing an accurate reference value for next-generation quantum technologies, this achievement is expected to contribute to the precise control and miniaturization of quantum devices, including atomic clocks and neutral-atom quantum computers. The work is published in the journal Metrologia.

articles.title: Universal electrical resistivity in iron-based high-temperature superconductors
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity ρ(T) in cuprate, iron-based, and nickelate superconductors represents one of unresolved problems in modern solid-state physics, because of the high absolute value of ρ(T), which, in many cases, exceeds the Ioffe-Rigel criterion, and a large difference in the ρ(T) shape for samples with different doping. Here I show that the nearest neighbors parallel resistivity model (arXiv: 2607.23484) can well describe the in-plane resistivity ρₐb(T) in iron-based superconductors (IBS) of type 11, 111, 122, 1111, 1144 and 42214 in which the spin density wave phase or nematic order is suppressed by doping. The model is based on the postulate that ρₐb(T) is a sum of two parallel conduction channels, where one channel is described by the Bloch-Grüneisen equation and the other by the Arrhenius hopping equation. Consequently, the variety of ρₐb(T) in the IBS is explained as a variation of the Debye temperature Θ_D and the hopping activation energy Eₐ. The derived Debye temperatures were used to estimate the electron-phonon coupling constant λₑ₋ₚₕin the studied IBS.

articles.title: Resonant suppression of the π-type Josephson component in a Kitaev-ladder junction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate Josephson transport through a finite normal segment connecting two Kitaev-ladder superconductors and show that discrete-level detuning controls the sign of the equilibrium Josephson coupling through a branch-selection mechanism. Away from resonance, detuning separates two competing low-energy branches, allowing inter-leg hybridization to clamp the 0-phase-favoring branch while leaving the π-favoring branch dispersive. The resulting negative first harmonic evolves from a branch-switching response at weak coupling into a smooth π-junction regime. At resonance the two clamping thresholds coincide, so the finite interval in which only one branch remains dispersive disappears. Once the inter-leg coupling exceeds the resonant clamping threshold, both low-energy branches become independent of the Josephson phase. The remaining finite-energy states then generate a 0-type Josephson coupling. At φ=π, the helicity decomposition yields an exact clamping identity for arbitrary finite normal-segment length. Within the controlled sweet-point finite-segment theory, serial propagation fixes the off-resonant fourth-order harmonic to be negative, whereas an isolated resonance leaves a positive residual harmonic within the resonant clamping regime. Numerical calculations demonstrate that the resonance-induced suppression persists away from the solvable phase choice. Thus normal-level resonance does not merely enhance Josephson transmission; it changes which low-energy branches contribute to the Josephson coupling.

articles.title: Quantifying the Kinetic and Thermodynamic Origins of the Glass-Forming Ability in Metals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The glass-forming ability (GFA) of a metallic liquid can be quantified by the critical cooling rate R_c, below which it crystallizes upon cooling. R_c is determined by the competition between R and the crystallization rate Kᵣₘ X. Here, we calculate R_c and Kᵣₘ X in model pure metals and alloys with BCC/B2 and FCC equilibrium crystal structures. Using classical nucleation theory and independently calculated crystal growth rates, we evaluate Kᵣₘ X=(IU³)¹/⁴ at T=0.8Tₘ, where I and U are the nucleation and growth rates and Tₘ is the melting temperature. We find a strong positive correlation between Kᵣₘ X and R_c over eleven orders of magnitude. We decompose Kᵣₘ X into a product of a kinetic contribution, involving atomic cluster attachment and diffusion, and a thermodynamic contribution. We show that the thermodynamic contribution to Kᵣₘ X dominates the kinetic contribution over the range of cooling rates that we consider. The nucleation barrier Δ G_c sim tildeγ³/Δtildeμ², where tildeγ is the reduced effective liquid--crystal interfacial free energy and Δtildeμ is the reduced bulk driving force, determines the magnitude of the thermodynamic contribution. The relative importance of tildeγ and Δtildeμ depends on the material: a large interfacial free energy can suppress nucleation in some systems, whereas a weak bulk driving force can inhibit crystallization in others. Analyses of the structural and chemical order show that better glass formers have enhanced structural frustration, more icosahedral-like and less crystal-like local environments, and a larger chemical-order mismatch between the supercooled liquid and crystal phases.

articles.title: Maximum-Temperature Theorem for a Nanothermometer
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The steady-state temperature predicted for an ideal point heat source diverges in conventional heat-conduction theory, but no physical thermometer measures a point value. We derive a sharp, shape-independent upper bound on the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor with thermometric volume Vₛ, placed anywhere inside a region enclosed by an isothermal reference surface. The bound requires only the total heat power generated in the region dotQ, a lower bound on its thermal conductivity κₘ, and the value of Vₛ. It is otherwise independent of the heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source--sensor distance. For dotQ=50~pW, κₘ = 0.1~mathrmW,m⁻¹K⁻¹, and Vₛ=10⁻²²,m³, approximately the volume of a 60~nm-diameter sphere, the theorem permits a maximum temperature rise of approximately 2~mK above the reference level. The result applies directly to nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer particles, and core-shell quantum dots. It shows that neither source localization nor uncertain source-sensor separation can account for kelvin-scale readings under steady-state heat conduction.

articles.title: Quantum state tomography through multi-frequency Josephson effect
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Macroscopic quantum effects emerge when the coherent behavior of countless microscopic quantum states manifests collectively at a visible scale, as exemplified by the supercurrent carried by innumerable finite-momentum Cooper pairs. By rigorously analyzing the time evolution of superconducting nanodevices including finite-momentum superconductors and quantum-dot Josephson junctions, we analytically derive the ubiquitous macroscopic supercurrent that originates from quantum interference between distinct many-body eigenstates, which we term as the dynamic interference supercurrent. The dynamic interference supercurrent in a system of two Andreev spin qubits exhibits multi-frequency Josephson effect in the absence of external voltage and is governed by the response of the many-body eigenfunctions (vert rrangle) to variations in the superconducting phase φ, determined by the φ-space Berry connection Cᵣᵣ'=langle r|partial_φ|r'rangle. The macroscopic dynamic interference supercurrent, an inherent property of the superposition state itself, enables an advanced quantum entanglement measurement of the Andreev spin qubits. These findings open new avenues for investigating superconducting nanodevice properties from a wave-function level, with substantial implications for advancing quantum science and technology in solid-state superconducting devices, such as quantum computer, communication, memory, and sensor.

articles.title: Calibrated shape-only recovery of membrane viscosities
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearby relaxation rates make two membrane viscosities difficult to distinguish from a shape transient. We show how calibrated preparation removes this loss of local sensitivity in a linear Kelvin-Voigt sphere with finite area elasticity and intrinsic membrane dissipation. Two independent releases, with a known signed amplitude ratio and calibrated relative gain and timing, yield normal-displacement records whose fixed linear combination separates the shear and dilatational rates. Their common amplitude remains unknown. For fixed sampling, positive-definite weights, bounded positive rates and nonzero excitation, the amplitude-projected sensitivity has a positive lower bound even at rate coincidence. Without relative calibration, the paired sensitivity decreases linearly with the rate gap; the single tangential-release record decreases quadratically. The calibrated bound is compatible with fixed finite initial energy. A positive local bound also persists with independent ratio calibration of fixed positive precision under a Gaussian error model. Supplied elastic coefficients convert the recovered rates into the two surface viscosities. An unbounded spherical Stokes extension quantifies how bulk dissipation changes the modal patterns and provides a sufficient full-Jacobian criterion for retaining local material sensitivity.

articles.title: Water-Driven Porous Silicon as a Platform for Blue Materials
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Living organisms control water to transport matter, transfer energy and drive chemical reactions. In this perspective, we argue that porous silicon can give engineering materials comparable control over water. Its pore architecture, surface chemistry and semiconducting skeleton can be shaped across length scales with the precision of semiconductor processing and, like the water it can host, it relies on one of the most abundant chemical elements on Earth. Liquids in porous silicon, most often water, can flow as a continuum through pores a few nanometers wide, strain the skeleton through capillary and electrosorption stresses, shift structural color, switch transparency, and modulate or generate electrical signals. We describe three directions to combine and extend these effects and overcome their limitations. Pore hierarchy resolves the classical trade-off between interface area and transport speed by combining large and small pores and thereby allows functions to be scaled from thin planar films to three-dimensional components. Surface modification becomes a design variable that tunes the interaction between water and the pore wall. It can be set locally and, with switchable coatings, on demand. Finally, pores only a few molecules wide alter the properties of water itself. In the absence of a bulk-like volume, water can become dielectrically anisotropic and highly conductive. Altogether, these steps turn porous silicon from a responsive material into an adaptive, water-driven material.

articles.title: Surface corrections and vortex energetics in the Thomas--Fermi limit of a self-bound unitary Fermi superfluid
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a spin-balanced unitary Fermi superfluid bound by an attractive 1/r interaction within an extended Thomas--Fermi density functional. Its large-particle-number limit is the Lane--Emden polytrope of index 3/2. We prove the leading gradient correction to the ground-state energy and strong convergence of the density amplitude. A rescaled surface problem predicts the next energy correction and the leading integrated density error. Matching a vortex core to the polytropic bulk gives the energetic threshold of a singly quantized central vortex, including the constant beyond the leading logarithm. Linearizing the same surface problem predicts a local energetic threshold for collective surface excitations that, in the natural TF frequency units, decreases more slowly with particle number than the central-vortex threshold. Radial stationary, spherical Bogoliubov--Poisson, and axisymmetric real-time calculations test the predicted energy corrections and vortex matching, and resolve finite-size surface-mode minima whose approach to the continuum surface coefficient is followed to Nsimeq4×10⁶. For the reference gradient coefficient the vortex constant is c₁=-0.535, and the surface Landau scale is 1.417,ω_K(hbarᵣₘ ₑff²/2Rᵣₘ TF)¹/⁶propto N⁻¹/⁹; sector energies at Nsimeq4.6×10⁵, computed after the fit, agree with the extrapolated vortex threshold to 10⁻⁴. These results distinguish the accuracy of the Thomas--Fermi bulk from the gradient physics that controls the surface and vortex core, and separate vortex energetics from the open problem of nonlinear vortex entry.

articles.title: Spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model. The model is solvable in the limit of a large number of fermionic modes on each site. For a small ratio of the numbers of modes on the two sites, we derive the free energy analytically and find a finite-temperature symmetry-breaking transition. This transition changes from continuous to first order as the number of fermions produced in each conversion increases. Numerical results show that both types of transition persist beyond this regime, with an order-parameter exponent close to 1/2 for continuous transitions.
